notes.plans: Castle, then play ...f5, and if White plays a random move like Bd2, chase the knight with ...f4, gaining a positional edge.

notes.explains: After ...f5, White's best is f4. Black should not play ...e4, which gives away e6 and d4 and allows a blockade, and the center can be undermined with g4. Instead, Black continues the plan of chasing the knight.
notes.teaches: Avoid overextending your center; a pawn break that creates weaknesses is often bad. Prefer to maintain a mobile center.
notes.plans: Chase the knight with ...Knight d7, and if White plays fxe5, recapture with the knight to get a great square on e5. If White plays Nc4, prepare ...b6 and ...Bb7, targeting d5.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Knight d5, Black can also play ...Knight b8-d7, and if White plays fxe5, Black recaptures with the knight, getting a two-pawn center and a passed pawn, with the bishop coming to b7 to target d5.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with a piece can give you a strong center and a passed pawn; use pieces to maintain central tension.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to b7, bring the knight to f6, and aim for ...d5 or ...e4 breaks if possible.

notes.explains: Against the bishop to g5, Black plays ...a6 and ...b5 with tempo, attacking the knight. If White takes on f6, Black should recapture with the g-pawn, not the queen, as queen takes is losing.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider pawn structure and king safety; recapturing with the pawn can be better than with the queen.
notes.plans: After ...b5, if the knight moves to d5, play ...f5 to undermine the center immediately.

notes.explains: In the main line, Black plays b5 to chase a knight, and White typically retreats to d5. Black then has a choice between Bg7 and f5. The move f5 immediately undermines the center, forcing White to defend the e4 pawn. After White plays Be3, Black plays Be6 to prevent White from playing e5, and after castling and exchanges, Black consolidates the center and eliminates the weakness on d5.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, a timely f5 can challenge White's central pawns and create dynamic play. Preventing White's e5 advance is crucial to maintaining central control.
notes.plans: Black aims to complete development, castle, and then proceed with central breaks like f5, while keeping an eye on the d5 square.

notes.explains: In a common line, White plays Bxf6 and Black recaptures with the bishop. Black is not afraid of doubled f-pawns because they can easily break the center. White's plan is to triple control d5 with moves like Nc2 and Ne3. Black's recommended move is Bb7, which forces the issue on d5: White must keep recapturing with a piece, otherwise the hole on d5 becomes irrelevant.
notes.teaches: Doubled f-pawns are not always a weakness if they come with central control and the ability to break open the position. Prophylactic moves like Bb7 can put pressure on key squares and force the opponent to commit.
notes.plans: Black will continue with moves like Ne7, preparing to challenge the knight on d5 and eventually play f5, aiming to open the position for the bishop pair.

notes.explains: After White plays Nc2 and Black plays Ne7, White has options. If White takes on f6, Black is fine and will play f5. If White plays Ne3, Black can play Bg5, forcing the issue. If White takes on e7, Black recaptures with the bishop to avoid losing tempo. The resulting position is equal, but Black has the bishop pair and dynamic chances if the position opens up.
notes.teaches: When facing a knight on d5, challenging it with Ne7 can be effective. Recapturing with the bishop preserves tempo and maintains piece activity. The bishop pair can be a long-term asset in open positions.
notes.plans: Black will castle and aim for f5 to open the position, leveraging the bishop pair for dynamic play.

notes.explains: In the main line, White snaps off the bishop on b7 with gxf3, giving Black full control over d5. The e4 pawn is hanging, and White's king is less secure. Black's key idea is to play f5 and d5 to break open the position and target the pawn on g2. White often plays Bd3 to defend e4, and Black can then play d5, which is very concrete.
notes.teaches: When the opponent grabs a bishop, the resulting pawn structure can give you control over key central squares. Breaking open the position can expose the opponent's king and create attacking chances.
notes.plans: Black plays d5 to open the center, with tactical threats against the g2 pawn and the white king. If White defends with f3, Black can take; if White plays exf5, Black has Ng6 and plays for the f4 square.

notes.explains: After Black plays d5, White often takes on d5, and Black recaptures with the queen. White must defend g2, as castling would be checkmate. White's best move is Ne3, but then Black's queen is hanging, so Black must be careful.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, concrete calculation is essential. Recognizing threats like mate on g2 and defending accurately is crucial.
notes.plans: Black should continue with moves that maintain the initiative, possibly exploiting the exposed white king and the weak g2 pawn.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian line, after Black plays d5 and White captures, Black recaptures with the queen. White must defend g2, as castling would allow checkmate and queen f3 would lose a pawn. The knight to e3 is the best defense, but then Black's queen is hanging and must move. Black's only weakness is the kingside structure, which White can attack with a4, but in this line Black can ignore it.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's king is stuck in the center and your queen is active, look for tactical threats like checks and captures that force them to defend rather than develop. A seemingly weak pawn structure can be acceptable if you have active piece play.
notes.plans: Black should move the queen to safety, then continue with rook to d8, threatening e4, and follow up with f5 to attack. If White captures on b5, Black can play f4 and save the bishop, aiming for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: In the Sicilian Sveshnikov, playing Bb7 is a good move because it fights for the d5 square and combines well with Ne7 and a later d5. It can surprise opponents and lead to quick wins if they are unprepared.
notes.teaches: In the Sveshnikov, the bishop on b7 supports the d5 break and is a flexible developing move that also prepares a central pawn push.
notes.plans: Black aims to play d5, followed by central expansion and active piece play.

notes.explains: Against the Rossolimo (Bc4 against the Sicilian), Black has many viable moves, including g6, e6, d6, Nf6, e5, Qb6, Na5, Qc7, a6, and even Nd4. The main lines often involve White taking on c6, but there are alternatives.
notes.teaches: The Rossolimo is not as forcing as the Open Sicilian; Black has a wide range of playable setups, so you can choose a system that suits your style.
notes.plans: Black should choose a consistent setup, such as the Bb4 system with g6 and Bg7, and be ready for White's main options.

notes.explains: In the Rossolimo, if White does not take on c6 and instead plays moves like Re1 or c3, Black can play g6 and Bg7, followed by e5, creating a Benoni-style setup. If White takes on c6, Black should recapture with the d-pawn to maintain a Maroczy Bind-like structure, making d4 unplayable for White.
notes.teaches: When facing the Rossolimo, you can transpose into a Benoni or Maroczy Bind structure, which gives you a solid but flexible pawn formation and limits White's central expansion.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nf6, Qe7, and possibly Nd7 to defend the pawns, then castle and prepare queenside expansion with b6 and a5.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian setup, after White plays d3, the d4 square is heavily defended by Black, making d4 unplayable for White without losing material. Black chooses Queen e7 to support the e5 pawn and prepare development.
notes.teaches: When facing a closed Sicilian with d3, Black should aim to control d4 and e5, often with pieces rather than pawns, to restrict White's central break.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to f6, then after White plays Nc4, play Nd7 to defend the e5 pawn and prepare to challenge White's knight.

notes.explains: In the critical line, Black plays h6 to prevent Bh6 and prepare Be6 by stopping Ng5. White plays Nh2 to prepare f4, but Black is not afraid. Black plays Be6 and castles queenside. When White plays f4, Black takes with the g-pawn, opening the bishop on g7, and then plays g5 to force the bishop to move, typically to g3.
notes.teaches: In the Rossolimo, Black's h6 is a multi-purpose move that prevents bishop harassment and prepares development. When White plays f4, Black should capture with the g-pawn to activate the dark-squared bishop and create counterplay.
notes.plans: After White's f4, take with the g-pawn, then play g5 to drive the bishop away, gaining space and activity on the kingside.

notes.explains: In the Rossolimo, White's main pawn break is f4. Black can meet it by taking on f4 and then playing g5, forcing the bishop to g3. Black's position is solid and even slightly better, so risky moves like f5 are unnecessary.
notes.teaches: When you have a solid position, you don't need to force complications; you can play straightforwardly and still maintain an edge.
notes.plans: Black can start a queenside attack with a5 and b5, exploiting the hook created by White's a4. This is a natural and safe plan.

notes.explains: If White castles kingside instead of queenside in the Rossolimo, the situation changes. Black should play slowly, and if White plays f4, Black can again take and force the bishop to g3, then play Ng6, gaining full control of the dark squares.
notes.teaches: The correct plan depends on the opponent's setup. Against kingside castling, a slower approach with dark-square control is effective.
notes.plans: After Ng6, Black has a pleasant position with strong dark-square control, and can proceed with natural development.

notes.explains: In the Closed Sicilian with Bb5, Black should play ...Nd4 to force the bishop to retreat. Then ...e6 and ...Nf6 lead to a normal position. A common trap is for Black to play ...d5 immediately, which loses to a tactical sequence involving Qh5 and Re1.
notes.teaches: Be aware of tactical traps in the opening. A move that seems natural (like ...d5) can be refuted by a temporary piece sacrifice.
notes.plans: Instead of ...d5, play ...a6 first to prevent the check on b5, then play ...d5 next move. This avoids the trap and allows Black to proceed safely.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian line, playing a6 before d5 is crucial because it prevents a later Bb5+ check. Without the pawn on a6, White can play Bb5+ after ...Nf4, forcing Ke7 and then Qg5 wins material. With a6, that resource is gone, so Black can safely play d5 on the next move.
notes.teaches: The move a6 is a prophylactic move that denies the opponent a key checking square for the bishop, making a central break like d5 safe. Always consider whether a preparatory move like a6 can neutralize an opponent's tactical resource before committing to a central pawn advance.
notes.plans: After a6 and d5, if White plays exd5 and Nxd5, Black can respond with Nxd5, and if White tries Nxd5, Black has tactics involving ...Nd4 and ...Qh5, leading to a winning position. Otherwise, Black continues development with Bd6 and aims for a normal Sicilian structure.

notes.explains: In the line after a6 and d5, if White plays Ba2 instead of taking on d5, Black develops with Bd6. The pawn on d5 is immune because of tactics involving Bxh2. This leads to a normal Sicilian position with a symmetrical pawn structure and Black has a bit more space.
notes.teaches: When the opponent declines a central capture, you should continue developing naturally, but be aware of tactical resources that make your central pawn safe. A pawn can be 'immune' if capturing it allows a devastating counterattack.
notes.plans: Continue development with Nf6, and consider playing h5 to gain space on the kingside. The position resembles a normal Sicilian with equal pawn structures, but Black's pieces are actively placed.

notes.explains: Against the Closed Sicilian with g3, Black copies White's setup with g6, Bg7, d6, and then plays for queenside expansion with Rb8, b5, and b4. The key difference is that Black's knight is on c6 behind the c5 pawn, giving more influence over e4. This setup is similar to a reversed English opening against a King's Indian.
notes.teaches: When facing a setup like the Closed Sicilian, Black can adopt a symmetrical setup and then strike on the queenside with b5-b4. The presence of a knight on c6 supports the b5 break and controls key central squares.
notes.plans: Play Rb8, b5, and b4 to gain space on the queenside. If White castles queenside, the advancing pawns become a direct attack. If White plays c3 to stop b4, Black can recapture and leave White with weaknesses like a hole on d4 and a tender b2 pawn.

notes.explains: In the Smith-Morra Gambit (White plays f4 after the Closed Sicilian setup), Black's plan is to play g6, Nf6, Bg7, and then choose between Bb5 and Bc4. Against Bc4, Black plays e6 and d5 to challenge the center. This is a standard reaction to Bc4 in the Sicilian.
notes.teaches: When White plays Bc4 in the Sicilian, Black can immediately challenge with e6 and d5, securing the f7 pawn and gaining central space. This is a thematic idea that works in many Sicilian lines.
notes.plans: After e6 and d5, if White plays something like exd5, Black recaptures with the pawn or piece and develops normally. If White castles, Black continues with development and aims for a comfortable game.

notes.explains: In the Sicilian, when White plays Bc4, Black's setup is to aim for e6 and d5, starting with e6 to secure f7 and prepare d5. If White castles, Black can play d5 to equalize easily.
notes.teaches: Against Bc4 in the Sicilian, Black should aim for the e6-d5 pawn break to challenge White's center and gain space.
notes.plans: After e6, if White castles, play d5 to equalize; if White plays e5, avoid d5 and instead play d6 to undermine the pawn center.

notes.explains: If White plays e5 after e6, Black should not play d5 because the pawn on d5 is weak and White's e5 pawn binds Black. Instead, play d6 to challenge the e5 pawn and open the bishop.
notes.teaches: When facing a bind, don't create a weakness; undermine the center with a timely d6 to free your position.
notes.plans: After d6, if White takes, recapture with the queen, leaving White with an f-pawn that is ineffective for attack.

notes.explains: The line f5 after e6 is bad for White but common. Black can take the pawn, and if White recaptures, d5 is almost winning. Black gets excellent development and bishops while White has no attack.
notes.teaches: Accepting a pawn when the opponent's compensation is insufficient can lead to a superior position; prioritize development and piece activity.
notes.plans: Take the f5 pawn, and if White doesn't recapture, continue development with Nf6 and Bg7, aiming for a comfortable game.

notes.explains: Against Bb5 in the Closed Sicilian, Black plays Nd4 to challenge the bishop. If White takes on d4, Black recaptures with the c-pawn, forcing the knight to move back to e2, where it is misplaced.
notes.teaches: In the Closed Sicilian, Nd4 is a typical resource to neutralize the bishop on b5 and gain time.
notes.plans: If White doesn't take, after castles, take the bishop with Nxb5, then play a6 and b5, and fianchetto the bishop to b7.

notes.explains: In the line after Bb5 Nd4, if White plays Bc4, Black should not play d6 because c5 and d6 are hanging. Instead, take on f3 first, then play Ne7 to cover the key squares, and later challenge the bishop and aim for d5.
notes.teaches: When the center is under pressure, prioritize safety and piece coordination over immediate pawn breaks.
notes.plans: After Nxf3 and gxf3, play Ne7, then castle, and prepare d5 or challenge the bishop with Nf5.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack, Black's setup with g6, Bg7, and later d6 and Rb8 is solid. The f-pawn for White is often useless in attack, so Black can calmly develop and aim for counterplay.
notes.teaches: Against the Grand Prix, Black can rely on a solid setup and the long-term potential of the bishop pair and central breaks.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously, fianchetto the bishop, and look for d5 or e5 breaks when the center opens.

notes.explains: In the Smith-Morra Gambit, Black can use a reliable setup to avoid the typical tactical traps. The key is to not fall for tricks and maintain a solid position.
notes.teaches: Against gambits, it's important to know a solid defensive setup and avoid greedily grabbing material if it leads to danger.
notes.plans: Follow the prepared setup to neutralize White's initiative and reach a comfortable middlegame.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack against the Sicilian, Black's long-term chances are at least equal, and the engine often evaluates Black as slightly better. The opening is not dangerous for a well-prepared Sicilian player.
notes.teaches: Do not fear the Grand Prix Attack; with correct setup, Black can neutralize White's attacking ideas and reach a comfortable middlegame.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously, avoid weaknesses, and aim for a solid pawn structure with chances to outplay White in the middlegame.

notes.explains: Against the Smith-Morra Gambit, a solid setup with Nc6, a6, and e6 covers key squares and avoids the typical tactical pitfalls. The move d6 is played to prevent e5 and avoid complications, keeping the position safe.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, you can decline the pawn and focus on solid development; preventing central pawn breaks like e5 is often more important than material.
notes.plans: Develop the kingside, castle quickly, and be ready to meet White's aggressive moves with simple, safe replies. If White plays e5, you can either take or harass the bishop with Nh5.

notes.explains: In the Smith-Morra, after White's typical setup with Qe2 and Rd1, Black can calmly play Qc7 and then f6, making e5 less scary. When White plays Rc1 and Bf4, Black has time to castle and then play Qb8, avoiding pins and tactics.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the most natural-looking moves are not forced; you can take time to consolidate and only move the queen when necessary, keeping the position solid.
notes.plans: Continue with simple development, castle, and then reposition the queen to a safe square. If White plays e5, you can either take or play Nh5 to chase the bishop.

notes.explains: If White plays Na4 to target b6, Black can respond with b5, giving back the pawn but gaining activity. After the tactical sequence, Black ends up with a slight edge or at least equality, with no tricks left for White.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, returning the pawn can be a good way to neutralize threats and reach a comfortable position. Tactical resources like b5 can solve problems.
notes.plans: After the exchanges, Black has a solid position with a slight edge, and White's attacking chances have been extinguished.

notes.explains: Against the Alapin (c3), Black can play d5, leading to an isolated queen's pawn (IQP) position after e5 and dxe5. Black must be careful, but if a good blockade is established, White's attacking chances fizzle out and Black is often slightly better.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the side defending against the isolated pawn must set up a solid blockade; if successful, the pawn becomes a weakness and Black's position is easier to play.
notes.plans: Develop actively with Bg4, then play e6, Nc6, and take on d4 when necessary. If White plays Nb5, simply retreat the queen to d8. Continue developing and aim to blockade the d-pawn.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian setup, White's early knight sorties like Na3, Bc4, or Nb5 are not dangerous; they don't threaten anything concrete and only cost time. If Nb5 occurs, Black can simply play Qd8, forcing the knight to retreat, leaving it misplaced.
notes.teaches: Don't fear aggressive-looking but harmless moves; continue developing naturally. If a piece attacks your queen, move it back to a safe square and the attacker has wasted time.
notes.plans: Continue with normal development: ...Nc6, ...Be7, ...O-O, and prepare ...d5 or ...e5 as the position dictates.

notes.explains: When White plays Be3 in the Alapin, it signals a threat to win the d4 pawn, so Black must take on d4. If White recaptures with the c-pawn, it creates a square on c3 for the knight, and Black can develop with ...Be7 and ...Qd6, setting up a blockade on d5.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a piece is attacking a pawn and respond by capturing or defending. In isolated queen pawn positions, trading queens and blockading the d5 square is a key strategic goal.
notes.plans: After ...Qd6, if White plays Qb3, castle and prepare ...Rd8, and consider ...Qb4 to trade queens and recapture with the knight on d5.

notes.explains: The delayed Alapin (with Nf3 first) transposes to the same line as the standard Alapin after ...d5, exd5, Qxd5. The move order does not change the resulting structure, so Black can treat them as identical.
notes.teaches: Recognize transpositions; if two move orders lead to the same position, you only need to prepare one set of plans.
notes.plans: Play the same setup: ...Nc6, ...d5, and follow the Alapin plans.

notes.explains: Against the delayed Wing Gambit (where White prepares b4), Black can play ...Nf6, threatening the b-pawn. If White advances b5, Black's knight can jump to d4, then e6, d5, b6, and finally d7, while White's pawns become overextended.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, you can often return material to gain time and force the opponent's pawns to overextend. A knight can make multiple moves if it ends up well-placed and the opponent's pawns become weak.
notes.plans: After the knight maneuver, Black has a massive advantage; continue with ...d6, ...e6, and consider aggressive moves like ...g5 or ...h5 to exploit White's overextended pawns.

notes.explains: In the Wing Gambit proper, Black can choose between active moves like ...g5 or ...h5, which the engine favors, or a more solid approach with ...Qe7, ...a6, ...b5, and a dragon-like setup with ...g6 and ...Bg7, targeting the c3 pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have an advantage, you can choose between the most principled aggressive continuation and a safer, more positional one. Both are valid; pick based on your style.
notes.plans: If playing solidly, play ...Qe7, ...a6, ...b5, ...g6, ...Bg7, and aim to exploit the weakness on c3.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian sideline, Black can choose a slower but solid setup with Qe7 and a6, undermining White's structure and preparing b5. This avoids the sharpest lines but keeps the position flexible.
notes.teaches: When facing sidelines, it's often better to play solid, flexible moves rather than committing to a sharp setup. Undermining the opponent's pawn structure can be a key long-term plan.
notes.plans: Continue with a6, b5, and fianchetto the bishop to g7, aiming to exploit the weakness of the c3 pawn.

notes.explains: Against the Wing Gambit, Black can simply decline the second pawn and play e5, defending the extra pawn. If White plays Bb2, Black can leave the e5 pawn hanging and develop rapidly with Nf6 and Nc6, gaining a development advantage.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, returning material or ignoring a pawn can be fine if you get rapid development and activity in return. Don't be greedy; prioritize piece play.
notes.plans: After Bxe5, play Nc6 to develop and attack the bishop, then recapture with the queen if needed, enjoying better development.

notes.explains: Against the Snyder (b3), Black can use a universal setup with Nc6, d6, and Bb5 to avoid committing to a specific plan. If White transposes to a Grand Prix-like position, Black plays Nf6 and e6, staying flexible.
notes.teaches: A flexible approach in the opening means not committing to a rigid pawn structure or piece placement. This makes it harder for the opponent to prepare.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, castle, and aim to win the bishop pair when the center opens up.

notes.explains: In the McDonnell (Grand Prix without Nc3), White's f-pawn is advanced but not supported by a knight on c3, so Black can play d5 immediately. If White takes, Black can recapture and later regain the pawn, while White is left with a poor pawn structure on f4 and c4.
notes.teaches: Pawn structures like f4 and c4 for the opponent leave holes and give up the center. Being down a pawn can be acceptable if you have a superior structure and activity.
notes.plans: Play d5, develop with Nf6, and undermine White's center. If White plays c4, respond with e6 to further attack the structure.

notes.explains: Against the Keres (or Caris) variation, Black can transpose to a King's Indian-like setup, but with a timely d5 strike before White's bishop reaches g2. This keeps the position equal and playable.
notes.teaches: When facing a setup like the King's Indian Attack, striking in the center early can prevent White from completing their ideal setup.
notes.plans: Play d5, trade pawns, and develop normally. White may play d4, but Black's position remains solid.

notes.explains: Against the Bowdler (Bc4), Black plays e6 and aims for d5. If White plays Bg5 to prevent d5, Black can play h6 to force the bishop to move, and if it stays on the diagonal, Black can later play Ne4 with tactical threats.
notes.teaches: When an opponent pins or prevents a central break, you can often challenge the piece with a pawn move like h6. Tactical motifs like Ne4 can exploit loose pieces.
notes.plans: Play e6, then d5 if possible. If Bg5, play h6 and then Ne4, creating threats against the bishop and potentially winning material.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian line, if White plays an early bishop to g5 pinning the knight, Black can respond with e6 and later d5, challenging the center. If White captures on c3, Black wins material.
notes.teaches: When facing a bishop pin on the knight in the Sicilian, a timely d5 break can dissolve the center and free the position, often leaving the bishop misplaced.
notes.plans: Play e6 and prepare d5, aiming to trade central pawns and activate pieces.

notes.explains: If White instead develops the knight to f3, Black can still play d5. If the center is traded, the bishop may become blocked behind pawns; if not, Black can capture on e4 and possibly misplace the white king.
notes.teaches: The d5 break is a key resource in the Sicilian, creating central tension and potential tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Play d5, then recapture on e4 if possible, aiming to expose the white king.

notes.explains: The closed Ruy Lopez is a major system in the Spanish opening, and the Chigorin variation (with ...Na5) is one of its key branches. The structure and strategic ideas are more important than memorizing exact move orders.
notes.teaches: When studying an opening, first understand the typical pawn structures and piece placements, then learn the concrete theory.
notes.plans: Begin by learning the basic moves of the closed Ruy Lopez, then focus on the Chigorin's characteristic plans, such as ...Na5 and ...c5.

notes.explains: The Chigorin variation begins around move 9, and the subtleties of the resulting pawn structure are crucial for both sides. Black's knight maneuver to a5 is a defining feature, aiming to pressure White's center.
notes.teaches: In the Chigorin, Black often plays ...Na5 to challenge White's bishop on b5 and prepare ...c5, while White typically aims for a central pawn break with d4.
notes.plans: For Black: develop pieces harmoniously, play ...c5 to attack the center, and prepare ...Nc6 or ...Nb6. For White: maintain the center and consider c3, d4, and Re1.

notes.explains: Practical training against a computer that can include non-book moves is valuable because it simulates real opponents who may deviate from theory, especially at lower levels.
notes.teaches: Instead of only memorizing lines, practice the variation against a flexible training partner to build familiarity and adaptability.
notes.plans: Use a training tool to practice the Chigorin from both sides, setting it to include non-book moves to prepare for offbeat replies.

notes.explains: The Chigorin Variation is a defense for Black in the Ruy Lopez, characterized by moves like ...c5 and ...Qc7, aiming for counterplay on the queenside.
notes.teaches: When studying an opening, it's important to have a reliable repertoire and good resources, such as books that cover both main lines and sidelines.
notes.plans: For Black, focus on the main ideas of the Chigorin: pressure on the c-file and central breaks like ...d5.

notes.explains: In the historical game, Chigorin's early deviations like ...Kh8 and ...Ng8 were not optimal; the best move was Nf1, preparing to reroute the knight.
notes.teaches: In the Closed Spanish, piece placement matters; the knight often goes to f1 to support the center and prepare f2-f4 or other breaks.
notes.plans: For White, aim for a harmonious setup, often with Nf1, to maintain central control and prepare an attack.

notes.explains: In the Keres game, Black's ...Bb7 was not the most precise; ...d5 is a more thematic central break, but ...Bb7 is playable. After ...cxd4, Black gets typical pressure on c2.
notes.teaches: In the Chigorin, Black should seek active counterplay, often by exchanging on d4 and then placing a rook on c8 to pressure the c-pawn.
notes.plans: For Black, aim to create pressure on the c-file and prepare ...d5 to challenge White's center.

notes.explains: In the Chigorin Variation of the Ruy Lopez, Black often plays ...Qc7, ...Na5, and ...c5 to pressure White's center and queenside. The move ...Bb7 is playable but not the most precise; having the bishop on d7 is more flexible because it avoids retreating after ...d5.
notes.teaches: Piece placement should anticipate future pawn breaks. Choosing a square that doesn't require retreating after a central push saves time and keeps coordination.
notes.plans: Black aims to play ...d5 to challenge the center, and if the bishop is on d7, it can stay active. White often reroutes the knight to f1 and then e3 or g3 to support the center and prepare f4.

notes.explains: In the famous Karpov–Unzicker game, Black's pieces became passive after ...Nd7, ...Nb6, and ...Nc4 exchanges. White closed the center, gained space, and dominated the queenside with the maneuver Ba7, doubling rooks on the a-file, then switched to a kingside attack with Ne2, Nh2, and f4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, you can switch wings. Closing the center and dominating a file can create a positional squeeze before launching a decisive attack.
notes.plans: White's plan: close the center, double rooks on the open file, then transfer the knight to h2 and play f4 to open the kingside. Black's pieces are left without useful moves.

notes.explains: The Closed Ruy Lopez begins with e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7. From move 5 to move 9, both sides play nearly forced moves, with White playing Re1 and Black often castling and preparing ...d6.
notes.teaches: In mainline openings, early moves are often automatic and must be known precisely. Understanding the purpose of each move (e.g., Re1 threatening e5) is crucial.
notes.plans: White will develop and prepare d4 or d3, while Black will complete development and aim for ...d6 and ...Bg4 or ...b5 ideas.

notes.explains: In the Scandinavian main line after e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5, the queen on a5 is the most active square compared to d8 or d6, but it also becomes a target and may have to move multiple times. This move reduces Black's flexibility compared to other queen moves, making White's play more forced and giving Black a clearer path to a desired middlegame.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for the queen in the opening, weigh activity against the risk of losing tempi to attacks. A less flexible but more forcing move can simplify preparation and steer the game into familiar structures.
notes.plans: Black aims to reach a setup with pawns on e6 and c6, bishop on f5, and knights on f6 and d7. White aims for knights on f3 and c3, bishop on d2 to unpin and gain a tempo on the queen, and bishop on c4.

notes.explains: Both sides can achieve their ideal setups without much interference in this main line, despite the Scandinavian's aggressive reputation. The early moves are calm, with no immediate battle, as each side develops according to a known pattern.
notes.teaches: In some openings, the first several moves are about reaching a desired pawn structure and piece placement rather than engaging in tactical skirmishes. Recognizing these 'system' openings allows for easier preparation and a clear middlegame plan.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nf6, Nd7, Bf5, e6, and c6. White will develop with Nf3, Bd2, and Bc4, then decide on a plan involving pawn breaks like d5 or f4-f5.

notes.explains: Black has a choice on move 5 between Bf5 and c6, both leading to the same setup. These are the main moves, while rarer options like Bg4 are possible surprise weapons but deviate from the main line.
notes.teaches: In a system opening, several move orders may transpose to the same desired setup. Knowing which moves are interchangeable and which are critical helps you navigate the opening flexibly.
notes.plans: Black will proceed with the standard setup regardless of the move order, aiming for the same pawn structure and piece placement.

notes.explains: Capablanca plays h5 to prevent g4, which would dislodge his knight, and also to create kingside expansion before continuing on the queenside. This is a multi-purpose move that restricts white's play and prepares further operations.
notes.teaches: In endgames, use pawn moves to restrict the opponent's pawn breaks and to create a plan on one side while keeping the other side flexible.
notes.plans: Black continues with h4 and rook to c6, preparing to double rooks and maintain pressure on the c-file.

notes.explains: White's position is difficult because even if the knight reaches e5, it can be chased away with f6, and once the knight moves, the d4 pawn becomes very weak and almost impossible to defend. Black's g6 move defends the knight and solidifies the kingside.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a centralized knight can be a liability if it cannot be maintained; pawn weaknesses become critical when pieces are forced to move.
notes.plans: Black maintains the pressure on the d-pawn and the c-file, while keeping the knight well-supported.

notes.explains: The rook on c6 prepares to double rooks on the c-file, and the king moves to f1 because there is no way to improve the position otherwise. The knight on d5 is strong, and the d4 pawn is weak and hard to defend.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a strong knight outpost, the pawns around it become vulnerable. Use rooks to double on open files and keep the king safe from checks.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring the weak d4 pawn and improve the rook placement.

notes.explains: Black plays a5 to eliminate the weakness on a7, then a4 to create an isolated pawn on b3. This creates a second weakness in White's position, which is a key endgame principle.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, create weaknesses on both sides of the board. Eliminate your own weaknesses first, then force the opponent to defend multiple targets.
notes.plans: After a4, exchange pawns to leave White with a weak isolated b-pawn, then target it with the rook and queen.

notes.explains: Black exchanges queens, simplifying to a rook endgame where the weak b3 pawn will fall. The rook on b6 forces the white rook to d3, where it is awkwardly placed and cannot defend both pawns effectively.
notes.teaches: Do not keep queens on the board just because they attack weaknesses; if the position is simple, exchanging into a winning rook endgame is often best. Rook activity is paramount.
notes.plans: Switch the rook to a6, then play g4 to break open the position and create more weaknesses.

notes.explains: The knight transfers to a5 to attack the b3 pawn, which can no longer be protected. White is tied down and cannot defend all weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is tied down, transfer your pieces to target the weakest point. A knight on a5 can be decisive if the pawn it attacks is undefendable.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring the b-pawn and use the rook to cut off the king, then win the pawn.

notes.explains: White gives up the b-pawn deliberately because there is no way to defend it. After the pawn falls, Black must convert the material advantage by keeping the king cut off and avoiding tactical tricks.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is lost, do not panic; focus on converting the advantage by maintaining activity and avoiding counterplay. Keep the opponent's king cut off to prevent active defense.
notes.plans: Win the b-pawn, then use the extra pawn to create a passed pawn and promote, while keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: In this rook and knight endgame, the white king is cut off on the first rank, which prevents it from supporting the pawns or stopping the black pawn's advance. The black rook and knight coordinate to keep the king passive while the pawn marches.
notes.teaches: Cutting off the enemy king is a decisive endgame technique: it converts a material or positional advantage into a win by eliminating the defender's ability to counterplay.
notes.plans: Black advances the passed pawn, using the rook to shield the king and the knight to cover key squares, forcing white to give up material to stop promotion.

notes.explains: The winning method involves improving the position on both sides of the board before making the final break. White has weaknesses on both flanks, and black methodically increases pressure until they become unbearable.
notes.teaches: In technically winning endgames, do not rush the breakthrough. First improve your pieces and king to maximum activity, then create threats that force the opponent to weaken further.
notes.plans: Continue to harass the weak pawns, bring the king to a dominant central square, and only then push the decisive pawn break.

notes.explains: In a balanced material position, black's piece activity is the key advantage. White has weaknesses, but black's pieces are more actively placed, which can be amplified by improving the knight.
notes.teaches: Do not be afraid to give up control of an open file if it allows your knight to enter the game with a powerful outpost. Piece activity often outweighs static advantages like file control.
notes.plans: Play the knight to c6, where it supports central pawn breaks and pressures white's weaknesses, while the rooks remain flexible.

notes.explains: When the opponent has a misplaced rook, trading rooks might seem natural, but it can relieve the pressure. Instead, keeping the rooks on and improving the knight maintains the initiative.
notes.teaches: In positions with a static advantage, avoid simplifying if it lets the opponent reorganize. Keep pieces on the board to exploit the opponent's awkward piece placement.
notes.plans: Maintain pressure on the c-file and central squares, using the knight to create threats that tie down white's pieces.

notes.explains: The tournament result shows a dominant performance: 13 out of 15 with no losses. This level of consistency comes from converting small advantages cleanly and avoiding unnecessary risks.
notes.teaches: A hallmark of great endgame play is the ability to convert a small edge into a full point without giving the opponent counterplay. Study such conversions to improve your own technique.

notes.explains: In rook endgames, a passive rook can be tied down by pawn advances, while an active rook creates winning chances. Here, the rook's placement and the pawn structure determine whose position is better.
notes.teaches: Rooks belong behind passed pawns and on open files; avoid tying your rook down to passive defense.
notes.plans: Improve rook activity and create pawn weaknesses in the opponent's camp.

notes.explains: Centralizing the king is often the most important principle in the endgame. A centralized king supports pawn advances and restricts the opponent's king.
notes.teaches: In endgames, prioritize king centralization before other piece maneuvers.
notes.plans: March the king to a central square like d5 to dominate the position.

notes.explains: When pieces are already optimally placed, improving the position may involve pawn moves that create outposts or remove targets. Here, a pawn move like g6 ensures no weaknesses and prepares a knight outpost.
notes.teaches: Look for pawn moves that improve your piece activity and eliminate potential targets.
notes.plans: Play g6 to solidify the kingside and prepare a knight outpost on f5.

notes.explains: Creating a weakness in the opponent's camp (e.g., a backward pawn) can be a long-term plan. Here, playing b5 targets the a5 pawn and creates a weakness on b2, which is favorable for the side with the better pieces.
notes.teaches: In endgames, trade off your own weaknesses while creating weaknesses in the opponent's position.
notes.plans: Play b5 to fix the a5 pawn as a target and then pressure it with rook and knight.

notes.explains: In rook endgames, having a more active king and better pawn structure can lead to a winning rook-and-pawn endgame. The side with the active rook and centralized king can often force the opponent into passivity.
notes.teaches: A rook-and-pawn endgame can be winning if your king is active and your rook is behind passed pawns.
notes.plans: Use the active rook to harass the opponent's pieces and then advance your kingside pawns.

notes.explains: A single king move can be the difference between survival and defeat. Defending key squares like c4 prevents the opponent from penetrating with their rook.
notes.teaches: In endgames, every king move matters; always consider defending critical entry squares.
notes.plans: Move the king to d3 to defend c4 and prevent the opponent's rook from invading.

notes.explains: In rook endgames, activating the rook and creating passed pawns is key. Here, the side with the extra pawn must avoid trades that reduce winning chances, instead using the rook to support the passer and keep the opponent's pieces passive.
notes.teaches: Do not rush to trade pieces when you have a material advantage; keep pieces to maintain pressure and convert the extra pawn.
notes.plans: Use the rook to support the pawn's advance, cut off the enemy king, and force the opponent's pieces to defend passively.

notes.explains: The decision to not take a pawn (d4) can be instructive: leaving it may restrict the opponent's bishop and keep the king safe, while the knight can be rerouted to a strong outpost like b5 to support the pawn's advance.
notes.teaches: Sometimes declining a material gain is better if it keeps the opponent's pieces passive and your own pieces active.
notes.plans: Transfer the knight to b5 to support the passed pawn and cut off the opponent's king and bishop from the queenside.

notes.explains: When the opponent's pieces are passive, you can take your time to improve your position. The bishop has no scope because of the pawn on d4, so the winning side can slowly improve the knight and rook before finally capturing the pawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames, patience is a virtue: improve your pieces to their optimal squares before committing to captures.
notes.plans: After improving the knight and rook, capture the d4 pawn and then use the extra material to win.

notes.explains: In a rook versus rook and knight endgame, the side with the extra piece must avoid unnecessary risks. Here, the winning side uses the knight to cover key squares and the rook to support the passed pawn, while the king stays safe.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a material advantage, coordinate your pieces to support the passed pawn and avoid allowing counterplay.
notes.plans: Use the knight to cover promotion squares and the rook to protect the pawn, while the king supports from a safe distance.

notes.explains: In this rook and bishop versus rook and knight endgame, White has a three-to-two majority on the kingside, while Black's four-to-three on the queenside is more mobile. White's f-pawn is hard to push because f4 would leave a weakness.
notes.teaches: When a pawn majority is blocked, look for ways to blast open the position and give your pieces more scope, even if it means a pawn sacrifice.
notes.plans: White plays h5 to open lines and create activity, targeting Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: After h5, the rook enters the hostile camp, attacking a pawn. Black can defend with rook g7 or f6, or capture, but capturing allows rook h1 to win the pawn back.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active rooks are crucial; a rook on the seventh rank can create serious threats.
notes.plans: White continues to pressure Black's kingside pawns, while Black tries to defend and consolidate.

notes.explains: Black makes a defensive move with the king, bringing it closer to the action, which is natural. White continues with rook h7, and if Black plays rook f7, bishop takes g6 wins.
notes.teaches: Bringing the king closer to the center of action is often important in endgames, but beware of tactical shots.
notes.plans: Black plays rook c6 to defend both pawns and target White's weakness.

notes.explains: White adheres to the principle of aggression in rook endings and plays g4, advancing the kingside pawns. Black's king h3 is natural, but after knight c4 and king g4, knight d2 is a good move; king g5 could run into trouble after a check.
notes.teaches: In rook endings, advancing pawns on the side where you have the majority is a key principle, but be careful of counterplay.
notes.plans: White continues to push the kingside pawns, while Black tries to create counterplay on the queenside.

notes.explains: White plays g5, an incredible move that creates a passed pawn, fixes the weakness on g6, and gives the rook squares. It also makes rook f6 impossible for Black.
notes.teaches: A pawn move can serve multiple purposes: creating passed pawns, fixing weaknesses, and improving piece activity.
notes.plans: White's g5 pawn becomes a powerful asset, tying down Black's pieces.

notes.explains: In the line with Bf4, after Rxe1 Qxe1, the pawn on e4 is immune because if Black takes it, White gets a strong attack. For example, ...Nxe4 Bxe4, and Black's pawns on c6 and d5 hinder development.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn is 'poisoned' because taking it allows the opponent to activate their pieces or create a lasting initiative. Recognize when material is not worth the positional damage.
notes.plans: White can continue with Nc3, and if Black tries to take on e4, White recaptures and enjoys a blockade on d5.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, White deliberately ignores material to reach a classic winning setup: king on f6, pawn on g6, rook on h7. From there, Black's pawns fall like ripe fruit.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity and king penetration can outweigh material. Sometimes it is correct to sacrifice pawns to achieve a dominant, mating-net position.
notes.plans: White aims to get the king to f6 and rook to h7, then use checks and threats to force Black's king into a corner and win the remaining pawns.

notes.explains: White again declines to take a pawn, instead moving the king forward. This is a frequently available finesse: passing by hostile pawns rather than capturing them, so that the king is protected from rook checks from behind.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, when your king is advancing, sometimes it is better to leave enemy pawns alone and use them as shields against rook checks. Capturing them can expose your king to harassment.
notes.plans: White continues to advance the king, using the enemy pawns as cover, while the rook supports from the side.

notes.explains: After the king reaches a dominant square, White's rook captures the c7 pawn, and Black's position collapses. White then uses simple king moves to create mating threats, forcing Black to give up more material.
notes.teaches: Once you have a dominant king and active rook, you can create direct mating threats that force the opponent to shed material. Simplicity is often best: just keep the threats coming.
notes.plans: White continues to press with king and rook, using mating threats to win all of Black's pawns and then promote.

notes.explains: Capablanca's endgame play looks natural, but it is extremely difficult because of the psychological barrier: players are conditioned to value material, so they rarely consider sacrificing pawns when there is little material left.
notes.teaches: In endgames, you must be willing to sacrifice material for positional or tactical gains, even when the material count is low. The value of activity and king safety can exceed a pawn or two.

notes.explains: In this position, Black is better because Black has targets and squares to infiltrate, while White's pieces have no way to increase their scope. White would like to play b3 to prevent Black's plan, but that creates weaknesses on c3 and a3 that are too much to bear.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a position, consider whose pieces have potential to improve. If one side has clear infiltration squares and the other has none, that side is better. Avoid creating permanent weaknesses to stop a threat if the weaknesses are worse than the threat itself.
notes.plans: Black prepares to trade off a key defender (the knight) and then use the rook to infiltrate. White must find a way to create counterplay without weakening the queenside.

notes.explains: White's position is cramped and full of potential weaknesses; any attempt to improve with b3 creates holes on c3 and a3, which Black can exploit.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's position is already weak, avoid moves that create new weaknesses; instead, find ways to increase piece activity and target existing weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade off key defensive pieces and then invade with rooks on open files, such as e4 and c4, to harass the king and queen.

notes.explains: The move Rc4 is strong because it prepares to trade knights and then bring the rook to e4, where it attacks the king, queen, and f4 pawn simultaneously.
notes.teaches: A single rook lift can create multiple threats; look for moves that improve your piece's scope and create concrete tactical threats.
notes.plans: After the knight trade, play Rc4 and then Re4, using the rook to dominate the position and force weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black plays a5 to block the queenside, preventing White from playing a4 and gaining counterplay. If White tries b3 to stop a4, Black can play ...Re7 and target the newly created weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Restricting your opponent's pawn breaks can be a key part of a strategic plan; if they weaken themselves to create counterplay, you can exploit the new weaknesses.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece placement and maintain the blockade on the queenside, then proceed with the planned rook invasion.

notes.explains: Black chooses Nf5, which leads to a favorable exchange. If White doesn't trade, Black can take and create a passed pawn on d5, enabling Rc2.
notes.teaches: When you have a well-placed knight, offering a trade can be strong if the resulting pawn structure favors you; always consider the consequences of the exchange.
notes.plans: After the knight trade, use the resulting pawn on d5 to support rook invasions and create further weaknesses.

notes.explains: After gxf5, White must not take on h5 with the queen because Black can respond with ...Rh8, winning. Instead, White defends f4 with Qf3, but Black continues with ...Kg6, blockading the f5 pawn and ensuring it cannot move.
notes.teaches: In endgame-like positions, blockading an enemy pawn can be a decisive strategic advantage; it immobilizes a pawn and creates a permanent target.
notes.plans: Black will now use the blockade to further restrict White, then proceed with the rook invasion on c4 and e4.

notes.explains: Black executes the plan of Rc4, and even if White tries to prevent it with Rd4, Black can still play Rc4, and after the exchange, the rook will land on e4 with decisive effect.
notes.teaches: When you have a clear plan, execute it with force; even if the opponent tries to prevent it, your threats can be overwhelming.
notes.plans: After the rook reaches e4, continue to target the f4 pawn and the king, forcing further weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's heavy pieces coordinate to create multiple unstoppable threats. The rook on d3 and the queen work together to target the enemy king and queen simultaneously.
notes.teaches: When you have a material or positional advantage, look for moves that create multiple threats at once, making it impossible for the opponent to defend against all of them.
notes.plans: Continue to press the attack by bringing the rook to the f-file or e-file, maintaining threats of mate and winning the queen.

notes.explains: Black's rook on d1 is so dominant that White is reduced to waiting moves. Any attempt to activate the queen or rook leads to immediate loss, either by mate or by losing material.
notes.teaches: In a position of total domination, you can often improve your position with quiet waiting moves while the opponent has no useful moves. This is a form of zugzwang.
notes.plans: Maintain the bind, improve the king's position, and wait for the opponent to make a weakening move before striking.

notes.explains: Black's rook on c3 is a powerful outpost, pinning the pawn and attacking the queen. The threat of taking the rook or advancing the passed pawn is decisive.
notes.teaches: A rook on the seventh rank or deep in enemy territory can be worth more than its material value if it pins pieces and supports a passed pawn.
notes.plans: Use the rook to tie down the opponent's pieces, then advance the passed pawn to promote.

notes.explains: Black's rook on f1 attacks the queen directly, and there is no good square for the queen to move to. If the queen moves, checks and further attacks win it or mate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is overloaded defending both king and material, a direct attack on the queen can be decisive.
notes.plans: Execute the final combination to win the queen or deliver mate.

notes.explains: The exchange French often leads to symmetrical, dry positions where neither side can easily create a passed pawn, and games frequently end in draws at high levels.
notes.teaches: To avoid this, black can choose an uncommon but sound setup that aims for active piece play and an unbalanced game.
notes.plans: Instead of the routine Nf6, black plays Nc6, followed by Bg4, Qd7, and O-O-O, seeking quick development and kingside castling.

notes.explains: In the exchange French, after e4 e6 d4 d5 exd5, black can deviate from the standard Nf6 with Nc6, which is a normal and engine-approved move.
notes.teaches: Uncommon but sound moves can be used to steer the game into less familiar territory and avoid well-trodden drawing lines.
notes.plans: Black's setup involves quickly developing the light-squared bishop to g4, queen to d7, and castling queenside, creating attacking chances.

notes.explains: The repertoire aims to avoid the typical French defense problems by choosing lines that are comfortable for black, even if not objectively better.
notes.teaches: When building an opening repertoire, prioritize positions that are practical and lead to the type of game you enjoy, rather than only seeking theoretical equality.
notes.plans: For every common white response (Nc3, Nd2, e5, exchange, KIA, sidelines), have a plan that keeps the game interesting and avoids dry symmetry.

notes.explains: In the Exchange French, Black's setup with an early bishop to g4, queen to d7, and queenside castling is a sound and dynamic plan, even if it's uncommon. The engine may slightly prefer White, but at practical levels, the resulting play is rich and fine.
notes.teaches: Don't shy away from unusual but sound ideas; they can lead to unbalanced positions where understanding matters more than memorized theory.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g4, queen to d7, and castle queenside, aiming for opposite-side castling and a race of attacks.

notes.explains: When White plays the natural bishop d3, Black can choose a move order with bishop d6 first, keeping the e-file flexible and avoiding blocking it with a later bishop e6. This preserves the option to develop the bishop to g4.
notes.teaches: Move order matters: delaying a bishop development can keep options open and avoid future weaknesses like a blocked e-file.
notes.plans: After bishop d6, meet knight f3 and bishop d3 with c3 and bishop g4, then queen d7 and queenside castling.

notes.explains: In the resulting opposite-side castling position, there is no concrete theory; play revolves around ideas. Black's knight on g6 can head to f4 or h4, and the c6 knight is ready to reroute to e7 in anticipation of a b5 pawn push.
notes.teaches: In dynamic positions without forced lines, rely on general principles: attack on the side where you have space, and keep pieces flexible to meet pawn storms.
notes.plans: Prepare a kingside attack with pieces like knight g6-f4/h4, while responding to White's queenside pawn advances by repositioning knights (e.g., c6-e7) and transferring pieces to the kingside.

notes.explains: In the Advanced French, Black should not avoid the main lines but embrace them, as they can lead to a small edge. The setup with knight c6 is thematic and leads to rich play.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the main lines are the best practical choice; don't avoid them just to be original, especially if they offer good chances.
notes.plans: Play the main lines in the Advanced French, aiming for a small but lasting advantage.

notes.explains: In the Exchange French, playing an early Nc6 avoids the boring symmetry of the normal exchange lines and creates unbalanced play.
notes.teaches: When facing the Exchange French, choose moves that maintain tension and avoid automatic symmetry.
notes.plans: Develop pieces actively and prepare to challenge the center.

notes.explains: In the Advance French, after e4 e6 d4 d5 e5, Black's standard break is c5, aiming to pressure the d4 pawn. The pawn chain suggests Black plays on the queenside while White attacks on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, it's easier to execute a pawn break on the flank where you have space advantage.
notes.plans: Play c5 and follow up with Qb6 to target d4 and hinder White's development.

notes.explains: After e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3, Black plays …Qb6. This move makes it harder for White to develop the bishop to d3, because if White plays Bd3, Black can capture on d4 and after exd4, play Bd7, leaving the d4 pawn vulnerable. The typical tactical trick of Bxh7+ is not available because the knight on c6 controls e5 and d4.
notes.teaches: A queen move to b6 can directly disrupt the opponent's development and prevent key attacking setups, such as the Greek gift (Bxh7+).
notes.plans: If White plays Bd3, capture on d4 and then play Bd7, targeting the d4 pawn. If White castles, Nxd4 wins a pawn.

notes.explains: If White tries to keep the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal with Bc2, Black can play Nb4, and after castling, Nxc2 wins the bishop pair. This is good for Black because the bishop on c2 was the one pressuring h7, and removing it relieves pressure on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to maintain a key attacking piece, look for ways to trade it off or force it to a passive square.
notes.plans: After Bc2, play Nb4 and if White castles, Nxc2, winning the bishop pair and preparing Rc8.

notes.explains: In the main line, White often plays Bd2 or Be2 instead of Bd3. Be2 is passive and doesn't concern Black. After cxd4 cxd4, Black can play Nh6, aiming for Nf5 to add pressure on d4. This resembles the Bayonet Caro-Kann, but without White's g4 push, so the bishop on c1 is stuck.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is passive, you can often improve your own pieces to put pressure on a weak pawn, like the d4 pawn.
notes.plans: Play Nh6-f5 to triple the pressure on d4, and if White doesn't take, continue with Nf5 and prepare tactical ideas like Na4, Qa5, Bd2, Bb4.

notes.explains: In this French Defense line, Black has a knight on h6 that can jump to f5, putting pressure on d4. If White doesn't take the knight, Black gets strong pressure on the d4 pawn, similar to the Bayonet attack in the KID.
notes.teaches: When a knight can jump to f5 to pressure a central pawn, it's a strong resource even if it seems offside. The pressure can force White into tactical concessions.
notes.plans: If White doesn't capture the knight, continue with moves like Nf5, Qb6, and Bd7 to maintain pressure on d4 and b2.

notes.explains: After White captures the knight on h6, Black can recapture with the queen, hitting b2 and the rook. If White plays Nbd2, Black can take on g7, then on d4, leaving Black with the bishop pair and a good position.
notes.teaches: When a bishop is captured, recapturing with the queen can create double threats (e.g., on b2 and the rook). This can lead to favorable simplifications.
notes.plans: If White plays Nbd2, take on g7, then on d4, and castle. If White plays Rook b1, move the queen to c3, and be ready to handle the b7 pawn.

notes.explains: Against the advance French, White's main move is a3. Black can respond with c5, playing a Chameleon Slav setup, aiming to castle queenside and fight for the b3 square.
notes.teaches: In the French, if White plays a3, Black can adopt a Slav-like structure with c5, avoiding White's kingside attack and creating queenside counterplay.
notes.plans: Play c5, then develop with Nbd2, Ba5, Bd7, Ne7, Rook b1, Qc7. Maneuver the knight to c8-b6-a4, and consider bishop a4 to fight for b3. Castle queenside.

notes.explains: In this setup, Black has many attacking ideas on both sides: f6, g5, bishop e7, doubling rooks on the h-file, playing for the g-file, or the b3 and a4 squares. The position is rich and complex, and Black scores well in practice.
notes.teaches: A static pawn structure can still offer dynamic play if you have multiple plans. Having more experience in a complex position can be a practical advantage.
notes.plans: Choose from the various plans based on White's setup. Aim to create play on the queenside with b5 or a4, or on the kingside with f6/g5.

notes.explains: In the French Defense, statistics show Black scores excellently despite the engine evaluation being slightly better for White. The main moves for White are Nc3 and Nd2, leading to the Classical, Winawer, or Tarrasch variations.
notes.teaches: Statistics can reveal practical chances that differ from engine evaluations; Black's high score suggests the French is a viable fighting opening.
notes.plans: As Black, choose a setup that avoids the sharpest theoretical lines and aims for a sound, positional game.

notes.explains: Against both Nd2 and Nc3, Black can play the Rubinstein Variation: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 (or Nc3) dxe4 Nxe4. This avoids the complexities of the Winawer and Tarrasch, leading to a position similar to the Caro-Kann.
notes.teaches: The Rubinstein is a way to sidestep sharp theoretical battles and steer into a more positional game where Black can outplay White through understanding.
notes.plans: After …Nd7 and …Ngf6, Black will develop the light-squared bishop to c6 or b7, aiming for a solid structure with no weaknesses.

notes.explains: The key idea is to activate the bishop to c6, avoiding a passive piece. Black may transpose to a Caro-Kann structure, play b6 and Bb7, or set up a double-bishop formation on d6 and c6 for a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: Flexibility in the opening: the same move order can lead to multiple viable plans, so understanding the typical structures is more important than memorizing exact moves.
notes.plans: Study games by players like Gelfand to see how to handle the various resulting structures.

notes.explains: After e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Nf3 Ngf6 Bd3 (or similar), if White exchanges knights on f6, Black should recapture with the queen, not the pawn. Taking with the pawn allows c4, which is devastating because the rook on e8 is stuck and d5 is coming.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider the resulting pawn structure and weaknesses. Here, taking with the pawn creates a weakness on e5 and allows White a strong central breakthrough.
notes.plans: Recapture with the queen to keep the pawn structure intact and prevent White's c4-d5 plan.

notes.explains: After the exchange on f6, Black sets up a threat to take on e4 and then on b7, forcing White to address it. White may play Be2, and Black continues with Bd6, a normal position. If White plays c4, Black can take on e4 with the bishop, getting an active piece.
notes.teaches: In these structures, Black should aim for active piece play and avoid creating weaknesses. The bishop on c6 is well-placed and can be traded or used aggressively.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously, play c6 to support d5, and maintain a solid pawn structure while seeking active piece play.

notes.explains: In the Rubinstein French, after the early exchanges, black's structure is solid with no weaknesses. The bishop can become active on e4, and black can support with c6, keeping the position clean and comfortable.
notes.teaches: Prefer clear, static positions with no weaknesses over sharp, double-edged play if you value safety and clarity. Active piece placement, like a bishop on e4, can compensate for a modest pawn structure.
notes.plans: Black will aim to complete development with c6, maintaining the solid structure and preparing to challenge white's center.

notes.explains: This repertoire is versatile, covering various structures: standard French, Botvinnik, Caro-Kann, exchange variation with opposite castling, and attacking positions. This variety prevents being stuck in one pawn structure.
notes.teaches: A well-rounded repertoire should include different pawn structures and plans, not just one. Learning ideas from players like Mikhail Botvinnik can help you handle diverse positions.
notes.plans: Study the ideas behind each structure, especially the Botvinnik system, to be prepared for any variation.

notes.explains: A repertoire that mixes standard French structures with other setups like the Botez system and opposite-side castling avoids being predictable and keeps the game rich.
notes.teaches: Don't restrict yourself to one pawn structure; versatility in openings prepares you for varied middlegame plans.
notes.plans: Use the repertoire to reach different structures and play according to their typical plans.

notes.explains: In the Schlechter Variation (Bd3), White aims to recapture on d3 with the bishop after ...exd4, getting a strong bishop. Black can neutralize this by playing ...Be4, forcing the bishop to f3, then ...c5.
notes.teaches: When facing a bishop that wants to dominate, challenge it early with a bishop sortie and then undermine the center with a pawn break.
notes.plans: After ...c5, continue with ...Nc6 and recapture on d4, then aim for ...Nd5 to block and trade pieces.

notes.explains: In the Steiner Variation (Nc3 d5 exd5 exd5 d4), Black gets an IQP position but with the bishop on c8 free, unlike the Caro-Kann. Black plays ...Bb4 to force White into an IQP structure.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the side playing against the pawn should blockade the square in front of it and avoid being attacked; having a free light-squared bishop is a key asset.
notes.plans: Develop with ...Bd3, ...Nf6, ...O-O, ...Nbd7, then set up a blockade on d5 and play against the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: Against the Chigorin (Qe2), playing ...d5 is bad because the pawn is pinned and the queen can be harassed. Instead, ...c5 transposes to a French-Sicilian setup, often leading to the Botez system.
notes.teaches: When a move like ...d5 is met by a pin, look for an alternative pawn break that exploits the opponent's queen placement.
notes.plans: Play ...c5 and treat the position like a King's Indian Attack, with the queen on e2 being a target.

notes.explains: In the Two Knights (Nc3 d5 Nf3), if White doesn't play d4, Black can play ...c5. Since White's knight on c3 blocks the c-pawn, White can't support d4 with c3, giving Black comfortable equality.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces block their own pawns, use that to create central tension and recapture on d4 with ease.
notes.plans: After ...c5, develop naturally with ...Nc6 and recapture the d4 pawn, reaching an equal position.

notes.explains: In the French Defense, when White plays an early Nc3, the d4 pawn is less easily supported by c3, so Black can challenge the center with c5. After White takes on d4, Black recaptures with the knight and later develops the bishop to c5, reaching an equal position.
notes.teaches: If White's knight is on c3, Black can play c5 to attack the d4 pawn, since White cannot reinforce it with c3. This leads to a comfortable equality for Black.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, recapture the d4 pawn, and aim for a standard French structure with pieces on c5, e7, and d6.

notes.explains: Against the Horwitz Attack (d4 d5 Bf4? or similar), Black can punish White's neglect of the center by playing d5 and then Bb2, attacking the d4 pawn. If White plays Nc3, Black develops Nf6 and Bb4, pinning the knight and threatening tactics. The pawn on d4 is immune because of a mating threat on d2.
notes.teaches: In sharp sidelines, Black must be alert to tactical resources like pins and mating threats to punish White's unnatural moves. Here, Black exploits the exposed position of White's king.
notes.plans: Exchange the dark-squared bishop with Ba3, then start a pawn storm with a5-a4, targeting White's king. If White captures on e4, recapture with the queen, using the pin to maintain material balance.

notes.explains: In the critical position after White castles, Black can play Qe7 and Ba3 to trade off the dangerous bishop. Then Black proceeds with a5-a4, creating attacking chances against White's exposed king. The engine may prefer White slightly, but practical chances favor Black due to the many tactical pitfalls for White.
notes.teaches: When facing an unusual opening, Black can rely on concrete tactical ideas and active piece play to create practical difficulties for White, even if the objective evaluation is slightly in White's favor.
notes.plans: Continue with the queenside pawn advance, keep the pressure on White's king, and be ready to recapture on b2 or play c5 to open lines.

notes.explains: In the Closed Ruy Lopez, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3, Black's ...a5 (the Keres Variation) is an uncommon move. Its original point was to prevent White's d2-d4 by gaining a tempo on the bishop, but this idea was refuted by Spassky in 1961, who showed that d4 can be played anyway. The move is rare today and generally gives White a pleasant position if handled correctly.
notes.teaches: When an opponent plays a move that seems to prevent a central advance, always check if you can play it anyway, often by ignoring the threat or using a tactical resource. A move that only prevents a central break may be too slow if the break is still possible.
notes.plans: For White, if facing ...a5, be prepared to play d4 despite the apparent pin on the bishop. For Black, if considering ...a5, be aware that it is not a reliable way to stop d4 and that other moves like ...Na5 (Chigorin) are more solid.

notes.explains: The Closed Ruy Lopez main line is characterized by White's c2-c3 and h2-h3. The move c3 is key because it gives the bishop on b3 a retreat square (c2) when Black plays ...Na5, and it also prepares d4 while restricting the c6-knight from jumping to b4 or d4. h3 is a prophylactic move preventing ...Bg4.
notes.teaches: In the Closed Ruy Lopez, White's c3 and h3 are essential prophylactic moves: c3 supports the center and gives the bishop a safe square, while h3 prevents annoying pins. Recognizing these standard moves helps you understand the structure.
notes.plans: After the main moves (e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 d6 c3 O-O h3), Black has many options, including ...Na5 (Chigorin), ...Nb8 (Breer), ...Nd7 (Zaitsev), and ...a5 (Keres). Each has its own plans.

notes.explains: The Keres Variation has a notable history: it was played without a clear plan by earlier players, then Paul Keres introduced it with deep analysis, believing it prevented d4. However, Spassky refuted it in a 1961 USSR Championship game, after which Keres abandoned it. Despite this, some later sources still considered d4 unplayable, showing that opening theory can lag behind practical refutations.
notes.teaches: Opening theory evolves through practical tests. A move that is refuted at the top level may still be effective against opponents who are unaware of the refutation. It's important to know both the historical context and the current theoretical status of an opening.
notes.plans: For players facing ...a5, study the Spassky game to see how White can successfully play d4. For players considering ...a5, be cautious and prefer more established lines like the Chigorin.

notes.explains: The Keres Variation (…a5) in the Ruy Lopez was originally designed to prevent White from playing d4, because after d4 exd4, a4, Bc2, Nb4 would win the bishop. This idea was refuted by Spassky in 1961 with the move d5, which gives White a strong bind on c6 and leaves Black's position unplayable if Black tries to take the bishop.
notes.teaches: A move that appears to gain a tempo or prevent a central advance can be refuted by a strong central pawn push that exploits the weaknesses created by the move. Always check if the 'threat' can be met by a more powerful central reaction.
notes.plans: After the refutation, White should confidently play d4 in this variation, and Black should avoid the Keres Variation altogether, as its main idea is unsound.

notes.explains: In the Closed Ruy Lopez, Black has several setups, each with a specific plan: the Chigorin (with ...Nd7 and ...c5) fights against d4; the Breyer (...Nb8, ...c5, ...Nc6-d7-c5) also targets d4 and improves the knight; the Zaitsev (...Bb7, ...Re8) pressures e4; the Karpov (...Nd7, ...Bf6) pressures d4; the Smyslov (...h6) prevents Ng5. These are all concrete plans to counter White's central space advantage.
notes.teaches: In closed openings, Black's plans are often directed against White's central pawns (d4 and e4). Each setup has a specific piece placement and a concrete idea, and understanding these plans is essential for playing the opening well.
notes.plans: As Black, choose a setup that suits your style and know the typical plans: pressure on d4 with ...c5 or ...Bf6, or pressure on e4 with ...Bb7 and ...Re8.

notes.explains: The moves h6 and a5 in the Ruy Lopez are similar in that both fight for control of f7. h6 prevents Ng5, avoiding a double attack on f7, while a5 pressures the bishop on b5, intending a4 to chase it away and also defend f7. However, a5 has the downside of undefending the b5 pawn, forcing Black to later play ...Bd7 to defend it.
notes.teaches: When comparing similar moves, consider both the immediate tactical benefits and the long-term structural or defensive weaknesses they create. A move that gains time on a piece may leave other pieces or pawns undefended.
notes.plans: If playing ...a5, be prepared to defend the b5 pawn with ...Bd7, and if playing ...h6, ensure that the kingside is safe and the rook can move freely.

notes.explains: In the Keres Variation of the Ruy Lopez, Black's a5 and h6 both aim to control f7, but a5 also pressures the bishop on b5, intending a4 to drive it away from the long diagonal. However, a5 leaves the b5 pawn undefended, forcing Black to later play ...Bd7 to defend it, which can become a target for White.
notes.teaches: When choosing between similar moves, consider which one creates more lasting pressure on the opponent's position versus which one creates weaknesses in your own. Here, a5 is more active but also more committal than h6.
notes.plans: White can exploit the undefended b5 pawn by applying pressure, often provoking it forward. Black must be ready to defend it with ...Bd7.

notes.explains: The Keres Variation is not objectively best for Black; after a5, White's strongest response is d4, which gives White a significant advantage. The main line involves a4, then an exchange on b5, with Black developing the knight to d7. This modern approach allows Black to delay the pawn exchange and aim for equality.
notes.teaches: Even if an opening is not objectively best, it can still be playable if you understand the resulting positions and have a plan for equality. The key is to know the critical lines and the typical middlegame plans.
notes.plans: Black should aim for a delayed Chigorin setup, with the knight going to a5 and then c4, while White tries to maintain pressure and a space advantage.

notes.explains: In the game against Unzicker, White again played Nxd4 after ...exd4, repeating the same mistake. This allowed Black to easily develop and achieve equality. The correct approach for White is to avoid this trade and instead play d5 or e5 to keep the pressure.
notes.teaches: Recognize recurring patterns in opening theory. If a move is known to be inaccurate, avoid it even if it looks natural. Always look for ways to maintain the initiative rather than simplifying prematurely.
notes.plans: White should aim for a central break with d5 or e5, while Black should look to develop the bishop to b7 and complete kingside castling.

notes.explains: In the Keres Defense to the Ruy Lopez, after ...a5, White's central break with d4 is a critical test. If Black recaptures with the knight on d4, White can trade knights, but Black's bishop to b7 immediately pressures the e4 pawn. Defending e4 with the natural Nc3 fails tactically because of ...b4, so White must use a different move like Nd2.
notes.teaches: When a central pawn is under pressure, the natural developing move may be tactically refuted; look for alternative defenses that maintain the pawn structure.
notes.plans: Black aims to maintain pressure on e4 and create play against White's center, while White seeks to consolidate and exploit the slightly better pawn structure.

notes.explains: In the resulting IQP (isolated queen pawn) position, Black's bishops on b7 and c5 make the pawn very dangerous. White's mistake was allowing the knight to remain on d5; taking it would have reduced Black's activity. Black's choice to play Nb4 instead of capturing on c6 was also acceptable, but capturing was stronger.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the side with the isolated pawn must be vigilant about piece activity; trading off the strong outpost knight can be crucial for the defender.
notes.plans: Black should aim to maintain the pressure on the IQP and use the active bishops to create threats, while White must seek exchanges to ease the defense.

notes.explains: When White chooses a different setup, such as playing a4 instead of d4, Black's task becomes harder. The move a4 prevents ...b4 and challenges Black's queenside expansion. In the games where White played a4, Black did not achieve the same success as against d4, indicating that a4 is a more resilient try.
notes.teaches: If a specific plan is working well for the defender, opponents will seek alternatives; be prepared for different move orders and setups.
notes.plans: Black must adapt to White's a4 by finding other ways to create counterplay, perhaps focusing on the center or kingside.
