notes.plans: After Qe2, black should continue with ...Qe7, maintaining the threat of ...Nxe4. If white tries to eliminate the knight with Bxc6, black recaptures with the b-pawn to prepare ...d5.

notes.explains: After white plays Bxc6 in the Jaenisch, black should recapture with the b-pawn, not the d-pawn. This keeps the d-pawn available for a later ...d5, and it also opens the b-file for the rook. White has given up the light-squared bishop, which is a key piece in the Spanish, so black has long-term chances.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn structure gives you the best long-term plans. Here, taking with the b-pawn preserves the option of ...d5 and creates pressure on the queenside.
notes.plans: Black continues developing with ...Nc6, ...Be7, and castles kingside. Then black can aim for ...d5, or maneuver the queen to c5 or e5 to prepare ...d5 and put pressure on white's position.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, black has several flexible plans. For example, the queen can go to c5 or e5, preparing ...d5. Black can also delay castling and instead play ...a5 to prevent b4, or ...Ba6 to pressure white's position. The pieces work together harmoniously, and black often has a slight edge.
notes.teaches: In open positions, look for ways to improve your pieces and create threats. Flexibility in move order can keep your opponent guessing and allow you to adapt to their setup.
notes.plans: Black can choose between queenside expansion with ...a5 and ...Ba6, or central play with ...d5. Eventually, black can develop the bishop to d6 and castle kingside, maintaining pressure on the f-pawn.

notes.explains: In this Anti-Ruy Lopez setup, Black's pieces coordinate well: the bishop on a6 pressures White's b-pawn and the f-pawn later, while the queen can become active. Taking the f-pawn is actually good for Black, and even winning the e-pawn instead is fine.
notes.teaches: When facing the Ruy Lopez, Black can aim for active piece play and pressure on White's kingside, rather than just equalizing. Even material grabs that seem risky can be good if they lead to active pieces.
notes.plans: Develop the rest of the pieces, consider Bc5 or Be7, castle kingside, and maintain pressure on the f-pawn.

notes.explains: After White takes on c6 and Black recaptures, Black can win the e-pawn. If White recaptures, Black plays Qd4, forcing the knight to f3, then Qe4+ regains the pawn with active bishops.
notes.teaches: In these structures, Black can use tactical tricks like Qd4 to regain material and open up the position for the bishops.
notes.plans: Develop the bishops to d6 and d7, castle queenside, and continue with kingside pressure.

notes.explains: In a specific line where White has played Nc3 and Black has taken on e4, Black should develop with Nf6. White's best is Qe2, and Black can pin the knight with Bg4, preventing Ne5 and preparing to castle queenside.
notes.teaches: Pinning a knight can be a useful way to restrict the opponent's piece activity and gain time for development.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e7 or d6, castle queenside, and aim for quick piece coordination.

notes.explains: In a position where Black has a bishop on g4 pinning the knight, White may try tricks like Qc4 to win the bishop if Black recaptures with the bishop. Black must be careful and use the rook to recapture, even if it costs a pawn.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are pinned, watch out for tactical shots that exploit the pin. Sometimes you must accept material loss to avoid worse.
notes.plans: If down a pawn, seek compensation through active pieces and counterplay, possibly with e4 and Bc5.

notes.explains: In the main line where Black has taken on e4, the pawn on e4 is attacked. Defending it with the queen is bad because White can play Nf6, gaining a tempo. White should defend with d3 or Nc3.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is attacked, consider developing moves that defend it and gain time, rather than moving the queen to defend.
notes.plans: After d3, Black can take on e4 and then play Nf6, leading to equal material and a playable position.

notes.explains: In the Jaenisch Gambit, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 f5, the e4 pawn is attacked. Defending it with the queen is poor because Nf6 will gain a tempo on the queen. The main defensive moves are d3 and Nc3, with d3 being a solid choice for Black and Nc3 preferred by White.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is attacked in the opening, prefer to defend with a piece that develops or with a pawn move that doesn't create weaknesses, rather than moving the queen out early.
notes.plans: After d3, Black can take on e4 and follow with Nf6, leading to a semi-open f-file for Black, which is a key source of counterplay.

notes.explains: The alternative to Bc5 is d6, but that is worse because it blocks the bishop and White can still win the pawn. After Nc3, Be7, Qd3, Black's best is to castle, even though it allows Qc4 winning the b-pawn. But the recommended move is Bc5.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, avoid moves that block your pieces or allow the opponent to win the pawn without compensation. Prefer active moves that create counterplay.
notes.plans: If Black plays d6, White can win the e5 pawn and Black has a bad position. So Black should play Bc5 to get active play.

notes.explains: In the Jaenisch Gambit, Black gives up the e5 pawn for long-term compensation: the bishop pair, pressure on f2, and an open f-file. If White does not take the pawn immediately, Black castles and the pawn becomes hard to capture.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing a pawn in the opening, ensure you get concrete compensation such as rapid development, open lines, or attacking chances against the king. A pawn sacrifice that leads to an overwhelming initiative is often worth more than material.
notes.plans: After the pawn sacrifice, Black aims to castle quickly and then build pressure on the kingside, using the open f-file and the bishop pair to force White to concede or defend passively.

notes.explains: The Marshall Attack and the Giuoco Piano Gambit (referred to as the 'gvi Gambit') both involve Black playing d5 and sacrificing a pawn, but the key difference is the knight's placement. In the Marshall, the knight is on c6, so after exd5 White gains a tempo by attacking the knight. In the Giuoco Piano Gambit, Black has already played d6 and then d5, and the knight is not on c6, so Black does not have to recapture and can instead play e4, gaining a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn sacrifice, the presence or absence of a piece that can be attacked after the capture can drastically change the evaluation. If the opponent's capture does not gain a tempo, the defender has more freedom to pursue their own active ideas.
notes.plans: In the Giuoco Piano Gambit, after d5 and exd5, Black plays e4, sacrificing another pawn but opening lines and gaining a huge initiative. Black's pieces are ready to join the attack, with options like Bf5, Bb7, Qd5, or c5.

notes.explains: In the Closed Spanish, Black has many viable setups (Chigorin, Breyer, etc.). In the Chigorin, after Bc2, the standard move is c5, but the Giuoco Piano Gambit instead plays d5, breaking in the center. This is surprising because it deviates from the main line, and the knight is not on c6, so White cannot gain a tempo by capturing.
notes.teaches: In well-known openings, a surprising deviation can be effective if it exploits a subtle difference in the position. Here, the absence of the knight on c6 makes the central break d5 more powerful than in the Marshall Attack.
notes.plans: After d5, Black aims to develop rapidly and create threats against the white king. If White does not take the pawn, Black can continue with moves like Re8, Bf5, or Qh4, building a strong attack. If White takes, Black plays e4 and gains a huge initiative.

notes.explains: In this line, if White captures the e5 pawn and Black recaptures with the d-pawn, Black has wasted a tempo by playing d6 and then d5, and the knight is not on c6, so Black can play e4 instead of recapturing. This is a pawn sacrifice that gives Black a huge initiative.
notes.teaches: When your opponent spends tempi on pawn moves, you can often sacrifice a pawn to seize the initiative and develop rapidly.
notes.plans: If White does not take the pawn, Black can continue with moves like Qd5, c5, Bb7, and e3, putting pressure on White's position.

notes.explains: After the pawn sacrifice, White's knight lacks a good square: e4 is met by Qd5, h2 is passive, h4/g5 allows Nd5 attacking the knight twice. White is forced to take the pawn, after which Black recaptures with the knight and then plays Bb7, leaving the bishop extremely active and the d-pawn hanging.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a poorly placed piece, you can use tactics to force them to make concessions, such as giving up the bishop pair or leaving weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will regain the pawn on d4 when desired, and the bishop can go to d6, c5, or f6, while the knight heads to c4.

notes.explains: If White plays d4, Black can simply take with the knight, and after Rxe5, Black recaptures on d4, leaving White with no compensation for the bishop pair. The engine evaluates Black as significantly better.
notes.teaches: Giving up the bishop pair without compensation is often a serious positional mistake, especially in open positions.
notes.plans: Black should aim to maintain the bishop pair and develop harmoniously, targeting the center.

notes.explains: In the main line, White plays d4, challenging the e5 pawn. Black should respond with exd4, and after Nxd4, Black plays c5 to undermine the knight. White continues developing with Bb7, Nd2, and Rc8, giving Black excellent piece play and a safer king.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn push, you can often break the center with a pawn lever like c5 to undermine the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Black will continue to develop, attack the center, and maintain pressure, with chances despite the engine's slight edge for White.

notes.explains: The Gajewski Gambit is a sharp response to the Spanish that starts like a Chigorin but diverges into aggressive play. It offers black dynamic chances even if the engine gives white a small plus.
notes.teaches: Choosing a less common but principled gambit can be a practical weapon to avoid mainline theory while still getting playable positions.
notes.plans: If you want to avoid mainline Spanish theory, consider the Gajewski Gambit as a go-to weapon.

notes.explains: The Marshall Attack arises after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5. Black sacrifices a pawn for long-term initiative and attacking chances. White often avoids it with anti-Marshall lines.
notes.teaches: The Marshall is a well-known pawn sacrifice for initiative; white players frequently sidestep it, so black must be ready for anti-Marshall systems.
notes.plans: If you play the Marshall, expect anti-Marshall lines like h3, a4, or d4; know how to handle them.

notes.explains: In the Marshall, after the main moves, black's queen goes to h4, creating immediate threats. White must respond accurately, e.g., with g3 and then Qh3, but black continues with Bg4 and other attacking ideas. A sample line shows black winning after white's inaccurate Nd2.
notes.teaches: In sharp gambit lines, one inaccurate move by the defender can lead to a decisive attack. Black's pieces coordinate to create mating threats.
notes.plans: If you are black, look for ways to maintain the initiative and exploit any defensive inaccuracies. If you are white, know the precise defensive moves to neutralize the attack.

notes.explains: The Berlin Defense (…Nf6) leads to the Berlin Wall endgame if white castles. Queens are traded, black gets the bishop pair, and white plays for a kingside pawn majority. It is notoriously drawish at top level but hard to play against at club level.
notes.teaches: The Berlin is a solid, irritating defense that avoids white's normal Spanish plans and can lead to a favorable endgame for black.
notes.plans: If you play the Berlin, be ready for either the endgame or other white options; if you play white, have a plan against the Berlin Wall.

notes.explains: In the Berlin Defense, if White castles, the queens are often traded, leading to an endgame where Black has the bishop pair and White has a kingside pawn majority. This is a well-known theoretical draw at the top level, but at club level it can be very tricky to play against.
notes.teaches: The Berlin is a solid, low-theory option against the Ruy Lopez that avoids the main lines of the Closed Spanish. It is not sharp, but it is reliable and can be used to sidestep heavy preparation.
notes.plans: If White castles, Black should be ready to enter the Berlin endgame with the bishop pair; if White avoids castling, Black should be prepared for alternative plans, such as an anti-Berlin with d3.

notes.explains: The speaker once tried an anti-Berlin approach with d3 in a tournament game, but lost quickly because the opponent knew a strong attacking idea that the speaker was not familiar with. This illustrates that the anti-Berlin can be dangerous for the unprepared player.
notes.teaches: When choosing a defense, consider your own experience and preparation. A solid, well-known line like the Berlin may be safer than an anti-line you have not studied deeply.
notes.plans: If you choose the Berlin, be ready for White's anti-Berlin tries, such as d3, and study the typical attacking ideas White has in those lines.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: In the Caro-Kann, after Black plays ...Nf6 and White declines the trade with Ng3, Black often tries to break open the position with ...c5, followed by ...b6 and ...Bb7. In this game, that plan was a mistake because it created a serious weakness on e5.
notes.teaches: When your opponent creates a pawn weakness, look for a weak square that the pawn move leaves behind. Here, ...b6 weakened control over e5, a key central square.
notes.plans: White can exploit the e5 weakness by playing b4 to gain tempo on the bishop, then Bb2 to pressure the diagonal, and eventually b5 to dislodge the knight that defends e5, allowing a knight to settle on e5.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: After Black's knight is driven to a5, White must choose a plan. The position is dynamic, and slow moves like Qe2, Rd1, etc., would allow Black to consolidate and create counterplay. The correct approach is to include more pieces in the attack immediately.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, you must act quickly and bring all available pieces into the attack. Slow, consolidating moves give the defender time to organize.
notes.plans: Play g5 to open lines for the queen and potentially trade off one of Black's key defenders with Ng4. This can lead to a devastating queen invasion on h5.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: In this attacking position against the castled king, the move g5 brings another piece into the attack and creates two concrete threats: it opens the queen's path to h5, and it prepares Nf6-g4 to trade off one of the key defenders of the black king. If the knight on f6 is removed, Qh5 becomes devastating.
notes.teaches: When attacking, count the number of attackers versus defenders on the kingside. If you have more attackers, the attack is justified; if you can trade off defenders, the attack becomes even stronger.
notes.plans: Play g5 to include the queen and prepare Nf6-g4, with the follow-up Qh5 if the knight is traded.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: The rook on f1 is passive and cannot help defend g7 or h7. The attacking side has five pieces aimed at the kingside against three defenders, but the ratio improves if defenders are traded. The move g5 also enables rook lifts like Rf1-e1 and then Re3, or even Ra1-a3 via a4, to bring more pieces to the attack.
notes.teaches: In an attack, bring every piece into the action. Rook lifts are a standard way to add attacking force, even if they take time.
notes.plans: Consider rook lifts to the third rank (Re3) or via a4 (Ra3) to join the kingside attack.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: The move Nh5 is a stronger way to trade off the defender than Ng4 because it clears the third rank for rook lifts and the knight on e5 is already well placed. It also unblocks the bishop, which is important for the attack.
notes.teaches: When trading defenders, prefer the move that improves your position in other ways, such as clearing lines or unblocking pieces.
notes.plans: Play Nh5 to force the trade of the knight on f6, then follow up with rook lifts and Qh5.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: The move Re1 is a strong preparatory move before deciding on the final attacking plan. It includes another piece in the attack and threatens Nh5, which would force the trade of the defender. If Black plays ...Bd6, then Nh5, Qxh5, f5, and Re3 follows, increasing the pressure.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet move that brings a piece into play is more precise than an immediate tactical blow. It keeps the opponent guessing and maintains the attacking potential.
notes.plans: Play Re1 first, then follow with Nh5 and rook lifts to the third rank.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: After Ng4, Black played Qd8, which defends f6 and avoids tactics on the e-file. If Black instead takes on g4, White recaptures with the queen, and Black's ...g6 weakens the kingside. However, ...f5 can block the position and equalize, though it is a weakening move.
notes.teaches: When defending, you can trade off an attacker, but be aware of the resulting weaknesses. Sometimes a pawn move like ...f5 can close the position, but it may be risky.
notes.plans: If Black takes on g4, recapture with the queen and prepare to exploit the weakened kingside; if ...f5 is played, reassess the attack.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: The move Ne3 is a strong regrouping move. It keeps the knight on e5, allows the knight to go to d5, f5, or g4 later, and prepares to trade off the defender on f6. After the trade, the knight can come to g4 with mating threats on g7 and h7.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a retreat is not a retreat but a regrouping. A knight on e3 can support multiple central and kingside squares, increasing its flexibility.
notes.plans: Play Ne3, then Nh5 to trade the defender, and later bring the knight to g4 for mating threats.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: When the opponent's queen leaves the defense of key squares, the knight can jump to h5, eyeing d5, f5, and g4. This creates threats against the castled king, especially if the queen can join the attack.
notes.teaches: A knight on h5 can be a powerful attacking piece, supporting sacrifices and creating mating threats on g7 and h7. Undermining the opponent's control of h5 can be a decisive mistake.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays a move like Qc7, consider Nh5, aiming for f5 or g4 to increase pressure on the king.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: After the queen enters the attack, the defender is often forced to make weakening pawn moves like g6. If the defender tries to block with f5, the attacker can sacrifice a knight to open lines, leading to a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When a king is under attack, pawn moves like f5 can create fatal weaknesses. Sacrifices to open the bishop's diagonal or to remove defenders can be decisive.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays f5, consider capturing with the knight, and if recaptured, recapture with the bishop to maintain the attack.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: A key maneuver is to bring the knight to g4, where it cannot be captured because the bishop is not blocked, and it creates threats of Qh6. This move can be decisive even if the queen is en prise.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece can be placed on a square where it is immune to capture due to mating threats. Look for such tactical motifs to increase pressure.
notes.plans: If the knight can reach g4, threaten Qh6 and prepare to exploit the pinned knight or other weaknesses.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: When the attack is underway, it's important to include all pieces in the attack. The rook on f1 can be brought to e1, not only to oppose the queen but also to support a rook lift to e3, which combines with knight f5 to create decisive threats.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, don't rush for a direct mate; instead, bring all pieces into the attack. A rook lift can be a powerful resource to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Play Rfe1, threatening Rf3 and Nf5, and if the queen moves, use the rook to support a decisive breakthrough.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: In this attacking position against a castled king, the knight on f5 is a decisive resource. It creates multiple threats: if the queen moves away, Qg5 followed by Qf6 threatens mate on h8; if the pawn takes on f5, recapturing with the bishop threatens mate on h7 and wins the queen if the bishop is taken.
notes.teaches: A knight on f5 near the enemy king can be a game-winning piece because it combines mating threats with attacks on the queen. Always look for such outposts when attacking a castled king.
notes.plans: If the knight is not taken, continue with Qg5 and Qf6 to force mate. If the pawn takes, recapture with the bishop and use the open g-file for the rook to join the attack.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: After the knight on f5 is captured by the g-pawn, the bishop on f5 threatens mate on h7. The defender's only way to prevent mate is to play ...f6, but then the rook can come to d3 or g3, adding more pressure. The rook on g3 creates threats of mate on g7 and h7, and if the defender tries to cover with the rook, it is pinned and the queen takes on h7.
notes.teaches: When attacking, bring all your pieces into the attack. A rook lift to the third rank can be a powerful way to join the attack on the king. Pins can be decisive in forcing mate.
notes.plans: Play Rg3, threatening mate on g7. If the defender plays ...Kh8, then Rg7+ and Rg6+ lead to mate. If the defender tries to defend with the rook, Qxh7+ is winning because the rook is pinned.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: In the game, after the knight on f5, the queen moved to c5, but then the rook came to c5, gaining a tempo on the queen. This shows that the attacker can use the rook to harass the queen and gain time for the attack. The final maneuver involves a queen sacrifice on h7, leading to mate with the bishops controlling the diagonals.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are more active, you can often use them to gain tempi on the opponent's queen, accelerating your attack. A queen sacrifice can be the climax of a mating combination when the remaining pieces deliver mate.
notes.plans: If the queen moves to c5, play Rc5, attacking the queen again. If the queen goes to e7, then Qxh7+ leads to mate. If the king goes to h8, then Rxf8+ and the attack continues.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: The preparation for the attack involved gaining tempi on the opponent's pieces, controlling the e5 square, and bringing more attackers to the kingside. The decision to trade off the g3 knight was part of the plan, and the knight on d5 was a key piece. The queen was allowed to go to h5, and the bishop was traded off, leaving the knight pinned with Qh6.
notes.teaches: A successful attack is built on small advantages: gaining tempi, controlling key squares, and coordinating pieces. Sometimes you must allow the opponent's queen to enter your position if it doesn't lead to a real threat, as long as you can continue your attack.
notes.plans: Continue to bring pieces to the attack, using the knight on d5 and the queen on h6 to maintain pressure. The final piece to join is the rook, which delivers the decisive blow.

notes.opening: Bishop's Opening: Vienna Hybrid, Spielmann Attack
notes.explains: This game was against the Caro-Kann, and the early ...b6 was dangerous. Playing ...b6 too early in such variations can weaken the queenside and give the opponent targets.
notes.teaches: Be cautious with early fianchetto moves like ...b6 in the Caro-Kann; they can be premature and create weaknesses. Understand the typical plans and timing of such moves.

notes.explains: In the f3 Nimzo-Indian, White's move f3 aims to control e4 and prepare a broad center with e4, but it is slow and weakening: it takes a natural square from the knight, delays bishop development, and does not help castling.
notes.teaches: When considering a move like f3, weigh the long-term structural gain against the immediate loss of development and king safety.
notes.plans: White intends to play e4 to establish a strong center, while Black should seek active counterplay to exploit White's lag in development.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4, Black's main replies to f3 are d5, c5, and O-O. The move ...Nc6 is a fair try but after d5, cxd5, exd5, e5, White's extra space pays off, and the knight on c6 is misplaced.
notes.teaches: In the opening, avoid placing pieces where they can be driven back or where they block your own pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Black should choose a move that challenges White's center or prepares to castle quickly.

notes.explains: After ...O-O, White plays a3 to force the bishop to capture on c3, gaining the bishop pair. Black then often plays ...Nh5 or ...Ne8 to prepare ...d5 or ...c5, anticipating White's e4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has the bishop pair, try to keep the position closed and avoid giving them open diagonals.
notes.plans: Black aims to break in the center with ...d5 or ...c5, while White will try to maintain the center and use the bishop pair.

notes.explains: The move ...Nh5 exploits the weakness of f4 and prepares ...f5, fighting for the center. White cannot play e4 immediately because of ...Qh4+; instead, White tries Nh3 to control f4 and g5, preparing g4 to punish the knight.
notes.teaches: When a knight goes to the edge, look for ways to attack it with pawns, but also be aware of the weaknesses it creates (like f4).
notes.plans: Black plays ...f5 to stop e4, and White continues with g4 to drive the knight away, leading to sharp play.

notes.explains: White's early f3 prevents ...e4, so Black's knight on h5 is not immediately challenged. White's Nh3 is a resourceful move, controlling key squares and preparing g4 to punish the knight's placement.
notes.teaches: When a pawn move like f3 weakens control of e4, a knight on h5 can be a strong piece, and the opponent may try to attack it with g4. Be ready to respond with moves like ...e5 to stop e4 and create counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should continue with ...e5, stopping e4, and if White plays e4 anyway, ...Qh4+ is a resource. Later, ...Bg5 can pin the knight, and ...Qe8 defends the knight on h5.

notes.explains: If White plays g4 to chase the knight, Black can respond with ...fg4, and after the knight retreats to f6, White may recapture with Qd3. However, opening the g-file with ...Rg1 can be dangerous for White, so Black should not take the pawn.
notes.teaches: Sometimes declining a pawn offer is correct if accepting opens a file against your own king. Here, ...d6 is a solid move, reinforcing the center and preparing to reroute the knight to f6.
notes.plans: Black plays ...d6, then ...Nf6, and later ...Nbd7 or ...Nc6, while White may develop with Bg2. The position is equal but Black's king is safer.

notes.explains: After White plays Bc3 and Black castles, White's bishop takes on f6, but Black recaptures with the rook. White's king is unsafe, and White hasn't achieved much with the central pawn majority.
notes.teaches: In the f3 Nimzo, Black can aim for ...Nh5, a key idea to pressure the bishop and create kingside chances. This move is a recommended resource against the f3 variation.
notes.plans: Black should consider ...Nh5, and if White plays Bc3, Black can follow with ...Bxc3 and ...Nh5, targeting the weakened kingside.

notes.explains: The main move is ...g6, preparing ...b6 and a hypermodern setup. White has moved many pawns but no pieces, while Black has castled and has a solid structure. Neither side has developed pieces by move 7, which is unusual.
notes.teaches: In hypermodern openings, it's okay to let the opponent push pawns while you develop and castle quickly. Black's strategy is to put pressure on the c4 pawn, which becomes a weakness after ...cxd4.
notes.plans: Black plays ...b6, ...Ba6, ...Nc6, and ...Na5, attacking c4. White must defend with Qe2 or Qc2, tying pieces down.

notes.explains: White's knight on h3 is well placed, heading to f2 to defend g4 and support the center. It can also go to g5 or f4. The e2 square is worse because it has fewer options.
notes.teaches: Knight placement matters: a knight on h3 can reroute to f2, g5, or f4, giving flexibility. Avoid placing knights on squares with limited prospects.
notes.plans: White plays Nh3-f2, while Black continues with ...Nc6-a5, pressuring c4. White may need to defend with Qe2.

notes.explains: If White plays c5 to defend the c4 pawn, it's bad because after ...dxc5, White's center is ruined, leaving weak pawns. Instead, White should play e5, and if Black takes, White can push c5 to resolve the tension.
notes.teaches: In a fluid center, you must be flexible. Avoid moves that weaken your pawn structure; instead, create pawn tension that you can resolve favorably.
notes.plans: White plays e5, and if Black captures, White recaptures with the bishop after Bf4. Black should play ...f6 to undermine the center, leading to complex play.

notes.explains: After White plays f3 in the Nimzo-Indian, Black often responds with f6 to challenge the center. White can meet this with Bf4, so that if Black captures on d4, White recaptures with the bishop, maintaining central control. This leads to a fluid, dynamic center where the pawn structure can transform in many ways.
notes.teaches: In dynamic central positions, be ready to recapture with pieces to maintain tension and flexibility. Understanding the possible transformations of the center is crucial before committing to such lines.
notes.plans: Both sides should look for opportunities to create or exploit weaknesses, often by capturing and recapturing in the center to see how the structure evolves.

notes.explains: In a specific line after f6, Bf4, cxd4, cxd4, Black plays d5. White's best is not to push the pawn (which would give Black a passed pawn) but to play cxd5, and after Bxd3, White gains a tempo with the queen. If Black recaptures with the pawn, White gets a passed pawn, so Black recaptures with the queen. Now White has many options, and the position is rich with possibilities.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn break, consider recapturing with pieces to avoid creating weaknesses and to gain tempi. Avoid pushing pawns that give the opponent a passed pawn.
notes.plans: White can develop actively, e.g., Rfe1 to control the e-file and prepare to advance or defend the e-pawn. Black should aim to challenge the center and coordinate pieces.

notes.explains: After the move c5, Black invites a structure resembling the Benoni. White typically responds with d5, and after castling and e4, Black plays e6, creating a Benoni-like formation. White plays Nf3, controlling f4 and preparing to bring the knight to f4 to pressure e6 and defend d5. Black plays b5, a typical Benoni move, attacking the c4 pawn. White must be careful because the c3 knight is pinned, and taking with the e-pawn would be dangerous with the king in the center.
notes.teaches: Recognizing transpositions to familiar structures (like the Benoni) helps guide your plans. In such structures, pressure on d6 and the c4 pawn is typical, and piece coordination is key.
notes.plans: White should develop harmoniously, aiming to control key squares and defend weaknesses. Black should seek active counterplay, often with b5 and pressure on the c4 pawn.

notes.explains: In the Benoni, Black often plays ...c5 to challenge the center before White consolidates. The d6 pawn is a typical weakness, so White tries to pressure it with moves like Bf4.
notes.teaches: When playing the Benoni, always be ready to put pressure on d6 and use ...c5 to create counterplay in the center.
notes.plans: Black should aim to maintain pressure on c3 and d4, while White tries to exploit the d6 weakness.

notes.explains: After White plays f3 against the Nimzo-Indian, Black often plays ...d5, and the main line involves ...c5. White cannot play e4 because the d5 pawn is defended twice, so play typically goes cxd5, Nxd5, and then ...cxd5.
notes.teaches: In the f3 Nimzo, ...c5 is a key move to create central tension and open the position before White consolidates.
notes.plans: Black should aim to open the center and create active piece play, while White must be careful not to fall into passivity.

notes.explains: After ...c5, White often plays e4 to gain a tempo on the knight, forcing it back to g7. If Black captures on c3, White gets a strong bishop pair and can harass Black's king.
notes.teaches: In these positions, don't fear tactical captures like ...Nxc3; instead, look for active moves like e4 that gain time and create long-term advantages.
notes.plans: White should develop actively, aiming for a strong bishop pair and attacking chances against Black's uncastled king.

notes.explains: In a later position, White plays a positional exchange sacrifice (Rxd5) to activate the bishop and restrict Black's options. This is a key idea in the mainline.
notes.teaches: Sometimes sacrificing the exchange for positional compensation (like a strong bishop and active pieces) can be the best way to maintain pressure.
notes.plans: After the exchange sacrifice, White should use the active bishop and pawn structure to create long-term pressure, while Black must find accurate defenses.

notes.explains: In this line, White's rook on d1 is sacrificed on d5, forcing Black to accept. White gets three strong central pawns in return, which are hard to stop unless Black gives back the exchange.
notes.teaches: Recognize positional exchange sacrifices that create a powerful pawn center; they can be worth more than material.
notes.plans: If Black returns the exchange, White's central pawns become mobile and can advance, creating threats.

notes.explains: After f3 d5, there is a known mainline with about 20 moves of theory leading to the exchange sacrifice. Black's options are limited: taking on c3 is never good, and Black must be precise.
notes.teaches: In sharp theoretical lines, knowing the mainline is essential; otherwise, you can be hit by a thematic sacrifice.
notes.plans: White should aim to harass Black's queen and drive the knights to the rim; Black should aim for e5 and Bishop e6, then prepare for the d5 sacrifice.

notes.explains: In the resulting position after the exchange sacrifice, Black has to play energetically to counter White's pawns. Moves like ...d6, ...Qc6, and ...Nf6 are typical, trying to blockade and prepare counterplay.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn center, you must create immediate counterplay or risk being overrun.
notes.plans: Black should aim to blockade the pawns and prepare to give back the exchange at the right moment to neutralize White's advantage.

notes.explains: White can continue with Rook g4, attacking the queen and creating threats. Even if White appears to lose a piece, tactics like Rook takes a5 and Bishop takes a7 keep the balance; the position is equal or slightly better for White.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, look for tactical resources that maintain the initiative even at material cost.
notes.plans: White should keep the initiative and use the passed d-pawn as a long-term asset; Black must play precisely to avoid losing.

notes.explains: Black has three main reactions to f3: castling, c5, or d5. Castling is recommended, leading to a different type of game; c5 enters a Benoni-like structure; d5 leads to the sharp exchange sacrifice line.
notes.teaches: When choosing an opening setup, consider which type of middlegame you prefer and whether you are prepared for the theoretical demands.
notes.plans: If Black chooses d5, they must be ready for the exchange sacrifice and the resulting pawn center; otherwise, castling is a safer practical choice.

notes.explains: The Dutch Defense begins with d4 f5, and can also be reached against other first moves like Nf3, b3, or c4. Its main upside is that Black immediately controls the e4 square, which becomes a weakness for White. The downside is that f5 weakens the f7 square and the diagonals toward Black's king, creating potential mating threats.
notes.teaches: The Dutch is a fighting, aggressive opening aimed at winning, not just equalizing. It is a system that can be played against many White setups except e4, where f5 is the bad Durras Gambit.
notes.plans: Black should build play around controlling e4 and launching a kingside attack, while being aware of the weakened dark squares around the king.

notes.explains: White's most common setups against the Dutch are either c4, Nc3, Nf3, and e3 (less common) or the more popular c4, g3, Bg2, and Nc3 with a kingside fianchetto. There are also alternatives like the Raphael variation, which resembles the London system with a bishop on f4 or g5 and a knight on c3, but without c4.
notes.teaches: Recognize White's main systems and the alternatives. In lines where White delays c4, Black should take the opportunity to control the center, as White's pieces are less active.
notes.plans: Against the Raphael variation, Black should aim to occupy the center, since White's c-pawn is blocked and d5 is only defended once.

notes.explains: In the Raphael Variation of the Dutch, White plays Nc3 and a bishop to f4 or g5, avoiding an early c4. This means the d5 square is only controlled once by the knight, and the queen also defends it, so Black can often play ...d5 early to stake a central claim.
notes.teaches: When White delays or avoids c4, Black should consider an early ...d5 to seize central space, even if it means a Stonewall structure without the usual ...e6 and ...c6.
notes.plans: Black aims for central control with ...d5, potentially forming a Stonewall setup, and should be ready for complex play.

notes.explains: The Hopton Attack is an aggressive try for White. Black has two critical responses: ...g6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop and challenge the long diagonal, or ...h6, immediately harassing the bishop. If White plays e3 after ...h6, Black should not take the bishop, as it would be a mistake.
notes.teaches: Against early bishop aggression, Black can either develop harmoniously with ...g6 or directly challenge the bishop with ...h6, but must be careful not to grab the bishop if it leads to a bad pawn structure or development issues.
notes.plans: Black chooses between ...g6 and ...h6 to neutralize White's pressure and develop quickly.

notes.explains: The Staunton Gambit (d4 f5 e4) is a pawn sacrifice that Black must accept. Declining leads to a lost position: if Black plays ...Nf6, White takes on f5 and Black is lost; if Black plays ...d6, White takes on f5 and Black's position collapses. After accepting, White develops sensibly and Black's king weaknesses become apparent, especially along the g5 diagonal.
notes.teaches: Against a gambit, sometimes you must accept the pawn and then carefully neutralize White's initiative, rather than trying to avoid the gambit at the cost of a worse position.
notes.plans: Black accepts the pawn and then must find accurate moves to survive White's attacking chances, particularly on the weakened dark squares around the king.

notes.explains: In the Dutch Defense, Black's early f5 directly challenges White's control of the e4 square, a key central outpost. This move also sets up a fight for the light squares, often supported by pieces like the bishop on b7 and the knight on f6.
notes.teaches: The move f5 in the Dutch is a direct claim on the e4 square, and Black's setup aims to control light squares. White often responds with g3 to fianchetto the bishop and contest those same light squares.
notes.plans: Black should develop harmoniously, aiming for moves like ...b6, ...Bb7, and possibly ...e5 to seize central control. White will try to undermine Black's center and exploit the weakened f7 pawn.

notes.explains: The Leningrad Dutch is characterized by Black's g6, fianchettoing the kingside bishop. This setup combines classical central presence (since f5 prevents White from playing e4 easily) with hypermodern piece play.
notes.teaches: The Leningrad offers Black the best of both worlds: a solid central pawn (f5) and a fianchettoed bishop. Black's main plan is to play ...e5 and control the center with pieces.
notes.plans: Black should aim for ...Nbd7 or ...b6 and ...Bb7, then ...e5 to dominate the center. White will try to exploit the f7 weakness and create counterplay.

notes.explains: The Classical Dutch (with ...e6) is flexible and can transpose to many setups, including the Queen's Indian. It allows Black to choose between a quick kingside attack (with ...Qe8 and ...Qh5) or a more solid development.
notes.teaches: The Classical Dutch is versatile and does not commit to a fixed pawn structure. Black can aim for a kingside attack or transpose to other openings, while White must seek queenside counterplay.
notes.plans: Black can play ...b6 and ...Bb7 to transpose to a Queen's Indian, or prepare ...Qe8 and ...Qh5 for a kingside assault. White should try to open the c-file and pressure Black's queenside.

notes.explains: The Stonewall Dutch features a solid pawn chain on light squares (d5, e6, f5), which is hard to break but leaves dark-square weaknesses. It can be dangerous for both sides, as it can lead to quick wins or losses.
notes.teaches: The Stonewall is a double-edged weapon: its pawn structure is solid but positionally suspect due to dark-square holes. Players must be aware of the resulting weaknesses and the potential for sharp play.
notes.plans: Black should look for attacking chances on the kingside, while White will target the dark squares and try to undermine the pawn chain. Both sides must be precise to avoid falling into tactical traps.

notes.explains: The Stonewall Dutch is built on a very solid light-square pawn chain, which is hard to break down. However, this solidity comes at a price: the dark squares, especially e5, become weak, and the light-squared bishop on c8 is permanently blocked by the pawns on d5 and e6.
notes.teaches: When choosing a pawn structure, consider the long-term weaknesses it creates. A solid-looking formation may leave permanent holes and a bad bishop that can be hard to fix.
notes.plans: Black typically aims for a kingside attack with moves like Qe8, Qh5, Nf6-e4, g5, Bd6, and Rf6-h6, trying to mate on h2. The knight on e4 is well supported and hard to dislodge.

notes.explains: Black's main attacking piece is the dark-squared bishop on d6, which supports the kingside assault. White's key defensive idea is to trade it off, often with Ba3, leaving Black with only the bad light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: In positions with a bad bishop, try to exchange the opponent's good bishop to accentuate their weakness. Conversely, if you have a bad bishop, protect your good bishop from being traded.
notes.plans: White should look for opportunities to play Ba3 to exchange the dark-squared bishops. Black should avoid this exchange and keep the bishop on d6 to support the attack.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack against the Sicilian, White avoids the open main lines and instead builds a kingside attacking setup. The engine may say Black equalizes, but White's practical attacking chances compensate for any theoretical edge.
notes.teaches: The Grand Prix Attack is a viable weapon at any level because it offers clear, consistent attacking plans even if it doesn't promise an opening advantage.
notes.plans: White will set up with f4, Nf3, Nc3, d3, castling kingside, and then Qe1 to prepare a kingside assault.

notes.explains: The move order is important: after e4 c5, White plays Nc3 (closed Sicilian), and if Black plays …Nc6, White can play f4 immediately, which is the Grand Prix. Alternatively, White might play Bb5 first and transpose later.
notes.teaches: Knowing the move order helps you reach your desired setup while avoiding unwanted transpositions.
notes.plans: After f4, White will continue with Nf3, d3, and castling kingside.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix, White's king usually castles kingside, even though the queenside is weakened. Black may try to pawn-storm on the queenside, but White's attack on the kingside is faster.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in attack, you can often ignore weaknesses on the opposite side of the board.
notes.plans: White castles kingside and proceeds with the standard attacking plan.

notes.explains: The key move Qe1 prepares Qg3 (or Qh4) to attack the kingside. This is a hallmark of the Grand Prix Attack.
notes.teaches: A queen can be repositioned to support a pawn storm or piece attack on the enemy king.
notes.plans: After Qe1, White will bring the queen to g3 or h4 to increase pressure on Black's king.

notes.explains: With pawns on c2, d3, and e4, White's light squares are well covered, but Black's knight could find a strong outpost on d4. Exchanging the light-squared bishop for that knight removes that danger.
notes.teaches: When your pawns occupy squares of one color, your bishop of that color can become 'bad'—exchanging it for an active piece is often a good plan.
notes.plans: White will aim to trade the light-squared bishop for Black's knight, especially if it heads to d4.

notes.explains: Black's main replies are g6 and e6. After e6, Black prepares d5, and may develop the knight to e7 or f6, or fianchetto the bishop to g7. White must react with Nf3 to develop and prepare castling.
notes.teaches: Recognize Black's typical plans and respond with natural development that also supports your own setup.
notes.plans: White will continue with d3, castling, and Qe1, while being ready to meet ...d5 with appropriate play.

notes.explains: The Scotch is an imbalanced, sharp opening compared to closed Spanish or Italian positions, offering dynamic play. This repertoire is based on Kasparov's lines from the 1990s, with some modern updates, though the Scotch is rarely played at the top level.
notes.teaches: Choose an opening that fits your style; the Scotch provides unbalanced, tactical battles rather than slow maneuvering.
notes.plans: Prepare to face the main responses: …Nf6 (Four Knights), …Bc5 (Classical), …Bb4 (Malanuk), and sidelines like Qh4, Qf6, and early trades on d4.

notes.explains: The most important structure from the Scotch arises after White trades on c6, leading to doubled c-pawns for Black. White has a central deficit because Black will play ...d5, forcing White to take, resulting in a structure with an e-pawn traded for a doubled c-pawn.
notes.teaches: Recognize key pawn structures and their typical plans; here, White aims to exploit Black's doubled pawns while Black seeks counterplay.
notes.plans: After ...d5, White takes and reaches a structure similar to an exchange Spanish or Berlin with queens off, where Black has no compensation.

notes.explains: The resulting structure after the pawn trade resembles an exchange Spanish or Berlin with queens off the board, giving White a pleasant endgame-like middlegame with no compensation for Black.
notes.teaches: When you have a structurally superior position, aim to simplify to a favorable endgame, especially if the opponent lacks active counterplay.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously, target the weak c-pawns, and prepare to convert the structural advantage.

notes.explains: The repertoire is not a theoretical overview but a recommended set of lines for White, focusing on the main variations and key structures. Practice is emphasized over rote memorization, using tools like Noctti for interactive training and feedback.
notes.teaches: Learn openings by playing them, not just memorizing lines; use training tools that give immediate feedback and allow you to practice specific positions.
notes.plans: Use the repertoire to play through the main lines, practice against a training partner or engine, and create flashcards or themes for positions you find uncomfortable.

notes.explains: In the Scotch structure where White has traded the e-pawn for Black's doubled c-pawn, Black's critical move is d5, forcing White to take and reach a structure with White having a doubled c-pawn. Although these pawns appear weak, they are difficult to target in practice, and the middlegame is roughly equal.
notes.teaches: When you have doubled pawns, they are not automatically weak if they are hard to attack; focus on the structural advantages you have instead.
notes.plans: White can play b3 to prevent pressure on the b-file and maintain a slight structural edge.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6, White chooses d4, the Scotch Game, which is a solid and underrated opening. Black's only good response is …exd4, and White recaptures with the knight. Black's best try for equality is …Qf6, but White can decline the queen trade with Qc4.
notes.teaches: The Scotch is a reliable opening that avoids the heavy theory of the Spanish or Italian, and White should be prepared to decline queen trades to keep the initiative.
notes.plans: White will develop naturally and aim for a central pawn majority, with typical plans involving f4 and e5 breaks.

notes.explains: In the main line of the Scotch, after Nxd4 Nf6, White plays Nc3, reaching the Four Knights Scotch. Black's most common and best move is …Bb4, pinning the knight and pressuring e4. Alternatives like …Bc5 or …Nxe4 are less challenging.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a piece pinning a knight to a pawn, be aware of the pressure on the pawn and consider how to relieve it or use it to your advantage.
notes.plans: White should be ready to meet …Bb4 with ideas like Nxc6 and Bd3, or if Black tries …Nxe4, White can take and then defend the knight on f3 to maintain the material advantage.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5, Black's bishop on c5 is not well placed; White can simply defend the e4 pawn with Bd3, and Black's attempts to win it (like Nxe4) are not challenging.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece placement is passive, you don't need to force tactics; just consolidate your center and develop naturally.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to d3, keep the pawn on e4 defended, and maintain a solid center.

notes.explains: If Black plays the piece sacrifice Nxe4, White can accept and then must meet the threat of ...Qe7 and ...d5 winning back the knight. White defends the knight and after ...d5, plays Bb5, forcing Black to deal with the pin before recapturing.
notes.teaches: When facing a piece sacrifice, the key is to identify the immediate threats and address them in the right order, often by creating counter-threats.
notes.plans: After Bb5, exchange on c6, castle, and enjoy a position where Black's king is unsafe and White has open lines.

notes.explains: Against the main line with ...Bb4, White takes on c6 with the b-pawn (not the d-pawn, which allows queen trades and leaves Black's king misplaced), then defends e4 with Bd3. Black must play ...d5 to undouble and challenge the center.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn structure gives you better long-term prospects; here, keeping queens on and maintaining a strong center is more important than pawn symmetry.
notes.plans: After ...d5, take exd5, and if ...cxd5, both sides castle, reaching a typical Four Knights Scotch structure.

notes.explains: In the sideline where Black castles and plays ...Re8, White can play Bg5, pinning the knight. If Black breaks the pin with ...h6 and ...g5, White sacrifices the e-pawn to play Qh5, infiltrating and creating a strong attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up a pawn is worth it to activate your queen and create lasting pressure against the enemy king, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: After Qh5, if Black plays ...Qf6, continue with Rae1, f3, and break in the center; if Black ignores with ...d6, increase pressure with Rae1.

notes.explains: The main line after ...d5 is exd5 cxd5, and both sides castle, reaching a standard Four Knights Scotch position. White has a choice here, with Bg5 and h3 being options.
notes.teaches: Recognize when you've reached a well-known tabiya; the early moves are often forced, and the real decisions come later.
notes.plans: Choose a plan from this position, such as Bg5 to pressure the knight or h3 to prevent ...Bg4.

notes.explains: In the Four Knights Scotch, after the main line moves, White reaches a familiar structure where Black's light-squared bishop is often awkward. Playing h3 prevents Bg4 and Ng4, forcing the bishop to b7 or similar passive squares.
notes.teaches: A prophylactic move like h3 can restrict the opponent's piece development, especially when the bishop has few good squares.
notes.plans: Follow up with Qf3 and Bf4 to challenge Black's dark-squared bishop and pressure c7.

notes.explains: White's setup with Qf3 and Bf4 aims to trade off Black's dark-squared bishop, which is often a key defender. Black's attempts like Qc7 are a waste of tempo because White will capture on d6 anyway.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is a key piece, trading it off can neutralize their defense and create long-term pressure.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...Rb4, respond with Bxd6, then develop with Rfe1, Rad1, Nd2, and Nf3 to occupy f5.

notes.explains: In the resulting structure, neither side has a clear advantage, but White enjoys a pleasant structural edge. If Black can eliminate the pawns, the position becomes equal.
notes.teaches: In the Scotch, White often plays for a small structural plus rather than a direct attack, and the engine evaluation may be modest but enduring.
notes.plans: Maintain the structure and avoid pawn weaknesses; if Black trades off the central pawns, accept equality.

notes.explains: In the Classical Scotch (…Bc5), White chooses Nxc6, the Kasparov variation. If Black recaptures with the bishop, White can develop with Bd3 and Qe2, leading to a favorable queenless middlegame.
notes.teaches: When a knight is attacked, capturing can simplify to a good structure, especially if it leads to queen trades.
notes.plans: After ...Bxc6, play Bd3, Qe2, h3, and then develop, aiming for a solid position with no dynamic compensation for Black.

notes.explains: Black's main response in the Classical is …Qf6, threatening mate on f2 and possibly recapturing the knight with the queen. White must defend the mate and choose the right square for the queen.
notes.teaches: When facing a threat, prioritize defense but also consider which defensive move fits your long-term plan, even if it temporarily blocks development.
notes.plans: Play Qd2 to defend f2, then recapture on c6, and continue development, accepting some congestion for a sound position.

notes.explains: After the opponent's move threatens mate on f2 and possibly recaptures the knight with the queen, the immediate priority is to defend the mate. Playing f3 would be disastrous, so the correct defensive move is queen d2, even though it temporarily blocks development.
notes.teaches: When facing a direct threat, address it with the most economical move that also maintains flexibility. Sometimes a move that appears to block pieces is justified if it sets up future tactics.
notes.plans: After queen d2, the knight is defended, and if the opponent recaptures with the queen, bishop d3 can be played, exploiting the queen's early movement.

notes.explains: The pawn on the knight is under pressure, so white must play dynamically. The move b4 chases the bishop, and after c4, the bishop is forced to retreat to d4, allowing knight c3 to defend the pawn. If the opponent takes on c3, queen d4 double attacks the knight, forcing it back, and then bishop g5 gives white a strong initiative with the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: When your pawn is attacked, use pawn pushes to drive back the attacking piece and create tactical opportunities. The bishop pair can be a powerful asset, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Continue developing and pressuring the opponent's position, using the bishop pair to cut across the board. If the opponent plays h6, consider b5 to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: After the opponent recaptures with the d-pawn, white continues with knight c3 and then plays the thematic knight a4, attacking the bishop. This is the Kasparov variation, aiming to grab the bishop pair and create attacking chances. If the bishop goes to d4, c3 and knight c5 follow, making it hard for the opponent to develop their light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: In positions with a central king, piece activity and the bishop pair can outweigh material or development. A knight on the rim can be effective if it forces the opponent's bishop to move and disrupts their coordination.
notes.plans: After knight a4, if the bishop retreats to d6, play f4 to push the pawns and keep the opponent's king in the center. If the bishop goes to e6, continue with the plan to chase it and build an aggressive setup.

notes.explains: In this Scotch line, White has chased the bishop away from its best diagonal and now wants to prevent Black from castling and developing easily. Moves like Qe3 and h3 are prophylactic, stopping ...Ng4 and keeping the king in the center.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, use tempo-gaining moves to disrupt the opponent's plans, especially their ability to castle and develop smoothly.
notes.plans: Continue with the aggressive setup: castle, then prepare f4 with Kh1, and aim to create a kingside pawn majority.

notes.explains: White's plan is to play f4 and push the e-pawn, creating a passed pawn. The pawns on f4 and e5 are assets, and trades generally favor White because Black's queenside pawn majority is weak.
notes.teaches: In positions with a central pawn majority, trades often favor the side with the majority because they lead to a winning endgame or a strong passed pawn.
notes.plans: Prepare f4 with moves like Qe2 or Qe1, and consider exchanging the dark-squared bishop to open lines. If Black takes on e5, recapture with the bishop and open the position.

notes.explains: In the Möller (or Møller) variation, after Bb4+ and c3, White plays Be3, aiming to take the knight on c6 and win a piece if Black doesn't retreat the bishop. Black must lose a tempo with Bb6.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are attacking multiple targets, the opponent often has to lose time to defend, which you can use to build a favorable structure.
notes.plans: Create a Maróczy bind structure with c4 and e4, and a knight on e3. If Black plays ...g6, exchange on b6 and then play c4 to prevent ...d5.

notes.explains: After the Maróczy bind is established, White's main idea is to prevent ...d5. If Black tries ...d5 anyway, White's king is still on e1, so Black might sacrifice a pawn to open lines.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, preventing the opponent's freeing pawn break is often more important than material. Be aware of tactical shots if your king is uncastled.
notes.plans: Maintain the bind, develop pieces to natural squares, and if Black plays ...d5, be ready to meet it with tactical play, possibly accepting a pawn sacrifice to keep the bind.

notes.explains: In this line, Black tries to generate counterplay with an early f5 break, but after the exchanges and castling, White's position is simply better. Black's attempts to force d5 are limited and not particularly dangerous.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has no clear plan, you should aim to complete development and castle quickly, maintaining a sound pawn structure and piece activity.
notes.plans: Continue developing harmoniously, keep the king safe, and prepare to exploit Black's weaknesses or lack of counterplay.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices a pawn with d5 to open lines against the uncastled white king, threatening queen h4 check. However, White can defend accurately and refute the sacrifice.
notes.teaches: When facing a piece or pawn sacrifice, it's crucial to find the precise defensive moves that neutralize the threats and leave you with a material advantage.
notes.plans: After defending, consolidate the extra material, coordinate pieces, and simplify if necessary to convert the advantage.

notes.explains: In a similar sacrificial pattern, Black tries knight takes e4 and queen h4 check, but White has a saving move (bishop d3) that attacks the queen and avoids the trap. Taking the knight would be disastrous, but there is a stronger move that wins material.
notes.teaches: Always look for active defensive moves that create counterthreats; sometimes the best defense is to attack the opponent's queen or other valuable piece.
notes.plans: After winning the piece, coordinate pieces to defend the weak points and prepare to convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Black's queen f6 aims at f2 with a possible bishop c5 mate threat. White responds with the aggressive knight b5, threatening c7, and after Black defends, White continues with knight c3, creating a strong bind.
notes.teaches: When the opponent attacks your king, sometimes the best response is a counterattack against their weaknesses, especially if you can create threats that are faster than theirs.
notes.plans: Maintain the pressure on c7 and d5, develop the bishop to e3, and prepare to castle queenside, keeping the initiative.

notes.explains: Black's queen h4 (Steinitz variation) pressures both f2 and e4. White chooses to sacrifice a pawn with bishop e2, allowing queen takes e4, but then plays knight b5, saving all pieces and creating strong threats.
notes.teaches: Sometimes sacrificing a pawn is justified if it leads to a lead in development and active piece play, especially when the opponent's queen becomes misplaced.
notes.plans: After the pawn sacrifice, use the lead in development to launch a direct attack, targeting c7 and the black king.

notes.explains: In this line, the knight on d4 is hanging, so White needs a different resource. The move bishop e2 offers a pawn sacrifice, and after queen takes e4, White can play knight b5, which attacks the queen and saves all the pieces.
notes.teaches: When your piece is attacked, sometimes a pawn sacrifice can buy time to activate your pieces and create counterplay.
notes.plans: After knight b5, if the queen takes g2, bishop f3 wins the queen. Otherwise, White can continue with knight c7 check or castle, depending on Black's response.

notes.explains: If Black takes on c3 with the knight, White recaptures with the pawn to maintain threats. Black is forced to play king d8, and White can castle, leaving Black's king misplaced.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with a pawn can keep pressure and prevent the opponent from consolidating, even at the cost of a pawn.
notes.plans: After castling, White can develop with bishop g5, attacking the queen and preparing to claim the e-file.

notes.explains: Against the Scotch, knight takes d4 is a poor move for Black. White can respond with queen f6, and then move the queen to c4, declining the trade and putting pressure on c7.
notes.teaches: Sometimes declining a queen trade can maintain pressure and target weak pawns.
notes.plans: If Black plays queen c6, White trades queens and gets a favorable pawn structure.

notes.explains: The move g6 against the Scotch is suboptimal. White can play knight c3, bishop e3, and after knight f6, take on c6 and play e5. The knight should not go to d5 because it gives up a pawn; it should retreat to g8.
notes.teaches: In the opening, avoid weakening moves like g6 that allow the opponent to seize central space and initiative.
notes.plans: White will continue developing and maintain the central pawn duo, while Black's position remains passive.

notes.explains: In the Petrov Defense, White can avoid the main line with Nxe5 by choosing sidelines like d4 (Modern Attack) or Nc3 (Three Knights). These moves are less common and can surprise opponents who expect the main line.
notes.teaches: Choosing less common but sound sidelines can be a practical way to take opponents out of their preparation, even if they don't offer a clear advantage.
notes.plans: Consider using d4 or Nc3 as surprise weapons in the Petrov.

notes.explains: After d4, if Black plays …exd4, White can sacrifice the pawn temporarily with Qxd4, followed by e5, driving the knight back. If the knight goes to d5, Qxd4 wins a piece; if it goes to f5, White gains time and has a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: Temporary pawn sacrifices can be used to gain time and activity, especially when the opponent's pieces are not well placed.
notes.plans: After …exd4, play Qxd4 and then e5, aiming to exploit the knight's lack of good squares.

notes.explains: In the line after d4 exd4 Qxd4 Nf6 e5, Black's knight is awkwardly placed on d5 or f5. If it goes to d5, Qxd4 wins material; if it goes to f5, White can capture on d6, removing the knight's outpost on e4. White ends up with a slight edge due to better development and an active queen.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are misplaced, you can often gain a lasting advantage by targeting them and preventing them from finding good squares.
notes.plans: If Black's knight goes to f5, capture on d6 and then develop with Nc3, aiming to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: The main move after d4 is …Nxe4. White should respond with Bd3, attacking the knight and preparing to recapture on e5. After …d5 Nxe5, White has an outpost on e5, similar to Black's on e4, but White has an extra move, giving them attacking chances.
notes.teaches: In symmetrical pawn structures, having an extra tempo can be a significant advantage, especially when both sides have attacking potential.
notes.plans: After Bd3 d5 Nxe5, castle quickly and aim to use the extra move to start an attack, possibly with c4 to gain space.

notes.explains: In the line with Bd3 d5 Nxe5, Black's best move is …Nbd7, exchanging knights. After Nxd7 Bxd7, White castles and then plays c4, gaining a spatial advantage. Black should respond with c6 to prevent White from gaining too much space.
notes.teaches: In open positions, playing c4 can be a useful lever to gain space and restrict the opponent's pieces, but the opponent must be ready to challenge it.
notes.plans: After castling, play c4 to gain space, and if Black plays c6, continue with development and prepare to exploit the space advantage.

notes.explains: In this Petrov line, White has an extra tempo and an outpost on e5, while Black's bishop on d6 and the symmetrical pawn structure on d4/d5 leave little immediate tension. White's main edge is the ability to play c4 early, pressuring Black's center.
notes.teaches: When facing symmetrical structures, look for the side that can advance a central pawn first to gain space and initiative.
notes.plans: White should aim to play c4, followed by Nc3, and castle quickly to exploit the extra tempo.

notes.explains: After the exchange on d5, Black ends up with an isolated pawn on d5, which is a target. White's own weakness on c3 is easily defended with Bd2, so White's structure is more solid.
notes.teaches: An isolated pawn can be a long-term weakness if the opponent can pressure it, but ensure your own weaknesses are easily defensible.
notes.plans: White should pressure the d5 pawn with pieces like Qf3 or Qb3, while keeping the c3 pawn protected.

notes.explains: In the sharp line with Qh5, Black sacrifices a pawn to create counterplay, but White can return the pawn to maintain a safer position. After Bxh6, Black must save both the rook and bishop, but cannot do both, so White wins material.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn sacrifice, sometimes giving back the material to consolidate is better than trying to hold onto it, especially if the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: White should continue to target the black king, using the open files and the bishop pair to maintain the attack.

notes.explains: In the Three Knights variation, Black's only way to stay in the Petrov is Bb4, but after Nxe5, Black is in trouble due to Qe2 ideas. White can castle and then choose between Bd3 or Be2, with Be2 being more solid.
notes.teaches: When your opponent deviates from the main lines, look for tactical refutations that exploit the loose pieces or the king in the center.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the extra pawn or at least a safe position, avoiding unnecessary complications.

notes.explains: In the main line of the Three Knights, after Be2, Black plays Re8, and White plays Nd3, allowing Black to recapture on e4. The resulting position has been played at the highest level, with balanced chances. White has doubled pawns but the bishop pair, yet the bishops are not immediately dangerous.
notes.teaches: Not every material imbalance is significant; doubled pawns can be compensated by the bishop pair, but if the bishops lack targets, the pawn structure may be more important. Evaluate dynamically.
notes.plans: Black will likely play d5 or d6, with d5 being the main move. White continues with Nf4, Be3, and Re1, aiming for normal development and an even game.

notes.explains: The Rossolimo Attack (e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5) aims to trade the light-squared bishop for the knight on c6, then play d3 to solidify the center. This reduces Black's typical Sicilian counterplay and leaves White with a sound but less dynamic structure.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, White can choose setups that limit Black's counterplay rather than maximizing immediate aggression. Trading a bishop for a knight to weaken Black's pawn structure or reduce activity is a common strategic idea.
notes.plans: White typically follows up with d3, castling, and later c3 or other solid development, avoiding overextension.

notes.explains: Black's early ...Nd4 in this position is ineffective because White can simply capture the knight, and Black's resulting pawn on d4 becomes a liability. White's development and castled king are more valuable than Black's extra central pawn.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn-grabbing or central thrust in the opening, weigh the cost in development and king safety. A pawn that is weak or easily attacked can be a long-term burden.
notes.plans: White can take the knight and then continue with d3 or castling, maintaining a solid position.

notes.explains: After Bb5, Black's most common response is ...g6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop and pressure the long diagonal. Since White has given up the light-squared bishop, the light squares around White's position may become weaker, especially if White plays d3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent trades off a bishop, consider how that affects the color complex. Fianchettoing can exploit the weakened squares, but White's solid setup can still be viable.
notes.plans: White can choose between castling or Bxc6, each leading to different structures. Black will develop the bishop to g7 and aim for central control.

notes.explains: If White plays Bxc6, Black can recapture with either the b-pawn or the d-pawn. Taking with the d-pawn opens lines for Black's pieces and solidifies the queenside, though it does not bring a pawn closer to the center.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn structure you want. Opening lines for your pieces and creating a solid pawn chain can be more important than central pawn presence.
notes.plans: Black will develop naturally and aim for play on the queenside or center, depending on the recapture chosen.

notes.explains: In the Closed Catalan, Black declines the gambit pawn with ...Be7, choosing solid development over material. The resulting structure often features ...c6 and ...d5, forming a semi-Slav pawn triangle that is hard to crack.
notes.teaches: When facing the Catalan, Black has two main approaches: take the pawn and enter sharp lines, or decline and aim for a solid, closed position. The closed approach avoids immediate tactical dangers and focuses on long-term maneuvering.
notes.plans: Black will develop the kingside first, then the queenside, aiming to play ...b6 and either ...Bb7 followed by ...c5, or ...Ba6 in some lines.

notes.explains: The semi-Slav pawn structure (with pawns on c6 and d5) gives Black a very solid position that is difficult to open up, preventing White from launching a quick attack. However, it also leaves the c8-bishop potentially bad.
notes.teaches: A key idea for Black in such structures is to free the c8-bishop by playing ...c5, often after ...b6, to place it on b7. If Black fails to achieve this break, the bishop remains passive and the position cramped.
notes.plans: Black should aim for ...b6 and ...Bb7, followed by ...c5, to activate the bishop and challenge the center.

notes.explains: In the Closed Catalan, the main pawn breaks are ...c5 for Black and e4 for White. When Black plays ...c5, White often responds with e4, and after ...cxd4, White recaptures with the e-pawn, leading to a symmetrical or central pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Understanding the typical pawn breaks is crucial: Black seeks ...c5 to free the bishop, while White aims for e4 to challenge the center. The resulting structure often resembles a Queen's Indian setup for Black and a Catalan for White.
notes.plans: Both sides should maneuver to achieve their ideal pawn breaks, with White preparing e4 and Black preparing ...c5.

notes.explains: The Closed Catalan leads to a complex positional struggle requiring knowledge of many ideas from different openings, making it popular at high levels but less so among lower-rated players due to its complexity.
notes.teaches: To play the Closed Catalan well, one must be prepared for a deep strategic fight and be familiar with typical plans from related openings like the Queen's Indian and Semi-Slav.

notes.explains: In the Closed Catalan, Black's early ...Be7 signals a willingness to enter a complex positional struggle. Black aims to build a Semi-Slav or Queen's Indian-style pawn center with b6, c5, d5, and e6, keeping the bishop outside the pawn chain, then trade central pieces to equalize.
notes.teaches: The Closed Catalan is a rich, theoretical opening that requires knowledge of many structures; it is popular at high levels but demanding for lower-rated players because of its complexity.
notes.plans: Black should aim to establish the pawn center and then seek exchanges to neutralize White's space advantage, while White should develop naturally with Bg2 and castling before committing to central action.

notes.explains: Playing Qc2 before castling in the Closed Catalan is tempting to prepare e4 and defend the d-pawn, but it allows Black's ...c5, exploiting the weakness of d4. After ...cxd4, Black has traded his c-pawn for White's d-pawn, reaching a comfortable reversed Grünfeld-like position with no issues.
notes.teaches: Premature queen moves can create weaknesses; here, Qc2 invites ...c5, giving Black easy equality or even an edge. It's better to follow the main line with Bg2 and castling.
notes.plans: White should avoid Qc2 and instead develop harmoniously with Bg2 and O-O, keeping the position flexible and avoiding the tactical tricks Black has.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...dxc4 in the Open Catalan, White responds with Qc2 to regain the pawn. Black's attempt to defend with ...b5 fails tactically: White can play a4, and if ...a6, then axb5 wins material; ...c6 runs into a5, again losing material. The only try is ...b4, but then Nbd2 attacks the pawn and the rook, forcing ...c6, after which Nxe4 leaves White much better.
notes.teaches: When trying to hold a pawn, look for tactical refutations; here, the b-pawn advance is punished by a4, and the resulting pin or fork wins material. Always check if the defender can be attacked.
notes.plans: White should proceed with Qc2 and be ready to punish Black's attempts to hold the extra pawn, aiming for a clear advantage.

notes.explains: Black's ...b6 in the Open Catalan is a weird move but not terrible; after Bg5 and ...Nd5, the bishops are traded, and White should stand slightly better.
notes.teaches: Even unusual moves must be met with principled development and exchanges that leave White with a small but safe edge.
notes.plans: White can play Bg5 to provoke ...Nd5, then trade bishops and maintain a slight advantage in the resulting position.

notes.explains: In this Open Catalan line, Black's attempt to play b5 fails tactically: after a4, the pawn cannot be defended, and recaptures lose material; b4 is the only way to hold, but then White can attack with a knight to d2, hitting the pawn and the rook, forcing c6, and after the knight takes on e4, White stands better.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advance like b5 is met by a4, check if the pawn can be defended or if recaptures fail; if not, the advance is simply bad.
notes.plans: If Black tries b5, punish it with a4 and then target the weak pawn with a knight maneuver to d2 and e4.

notes.explains: Black's b6 is a weird but not terrible move; after White plays Bg5 and Nd5, the bishops get traded, White recaptures the c4 pawn, and Black is left with a weakness on c7. Playing c5 would create an isolated c-pawn, so White keeps a slight edge.
notes.teaches: When the opponent plays a flexible move like b6, look to trade off the bishops and recapture the pawn, leaving the opponent with a structural weakness.
notes.plans: After b6, play Bg5 and Nd5 to force trades, then recapture on c4 and aim to exploit the c7 weakness.

notes.explains: Black's c6 is the normal Open Catalan move, and White simply grabs the pawn back. After b5, White can play Qc2, which is a known setup. Black then tries to liquidate the center and make the position symmetrical, but White's bishop is better.
notes.teaches: In the Open Catalan, if White can recapture the c4 pawn and keep a better bishop, the position is slightly better even if the structure becomes symmetrical.
notes.plans: After c6, recapture on c4, and if b5 comes, play Qc2 to maintain control.

notes.explains: Black's main move is a6, which leads to main-line Open Catalan positions. White responds with a4 to prevent b5, then Black plays Bd7 preparing Bc6. White recaptures the pawn, and after Bg5, White holds a slight edge. There is a forced line with Bd5 and Be4 where the queen gets pushed around, but White ends up better.
notes.teaches: When Black plays a6, the standard response is a4 to stop b5, then recapture the c4 pawn; the resulting positions are known and slightly better for White.
notes.plans: After a6, play a4, recapture on c4, and develop with Bg5, keeping a slight edge.

notes.explains: After d5xc4, Black's a6 is the only good move; White responds with a4, prevents b5, and recaptures the pawn. In Open Catalan positions, if White gets the pawn back, he is usually better.
notes.teaches: In the Open Catalan, regaining the c4 pawn is a key achievement; if you can do so while keeping the position under control, you should be better.
