notes.explains: In the Bayonet line, White tries to exploit the weak g6 square by provoking h5 and then playing Bd3. If Black retreats the bishop, White can win material, so Black must exchange queens with Qxd3. Then after Qg6, Black plays Qd6 and Kd8, running to c7.
notes.teaches: When your king is in the center, you must be willing to move it to safety even if it looks unusual. Also, exchanging queens can be the right way to neutralize an attack, especially if your king can find shelter.
notes.plans: After Kd8, continue with Nd7 and e5, aiming to trade off the doubled pawns and reach a favorable endgame.

notes.explains: If White plays Bg5 in the Bayonet line, Black should not play Qb4 because it runs into Nd2 and the rook to b1, which is losing. Instead, Black plays Nf6, preparing e5. If White plays f4 before Bg5, Black plays e5 anyway, and if the pawn is taken, Black recaptures with the queen, and the position is fine.
notes.teaches: In sharp lines, you must be precise about which tactical resources are available. A move that works in one position may fail in another due to a single defensive resource. Always check for counter-tactics before grabbing pawns.
notes.plans: Play Nf6 and then e5, eliminating the doubled pawns and leaving White overextended. Black will have a comfortable position with an extra pawn.

notes.explains: Against the Van der Wiel variation (Nc3, g4, Bg6, Ng2), the main move is c5. This is a standard Caro-Kann idea to challenge White's center.
notes.teaches: When facing a setup that aims to demolish your kingside, counter in the center with c5. This is a typical pawn break in the Caro-Kann to undermine White's pawn chain.
notes.plans: Play c5 and continue with normal Caro-Kann development, seeking to open the center and neutralize White's kingside ambitions.

notes.explains: In the Caro-Kann, against the Bayonet attack, Black can take on e6, leaving Black with no weaknesses and an extra pawn.
notes.teaches: When facing a sharp attacking setup, simplifying to a position with no weaknesses and a material advantage is a reliable way to neutralize the attack.
notes.plans: Consolidate the extra pawn and avoid unnecessary complications.

notes.explains: Against the Fantasy variation, Black can play e6, then later take on e4 and play e5, aiming for a setup with bishop e6 to prevent White's typical attacking ideas like bishop c4.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy, Black can avoid the mainline attacking positions by choosing a move order that prevents White's most dangerous plans, such as bishop c4.
notes.plans: After bishop e6, if White plays c3, Black plays knight d7, preparing to meet knight g5 with h6 and queen h4 check if taken.

notes.explains: In the Two Knights variation, Black can play g6, aiming to transpose into the Gurgenidze system with a bishop on g7. This is rare and can confuse opponents who expect standard Caro-Kann setups.
notes.teaches: Choosing a rare but sound setup can take opponents out of their preparation and lead to comfortable positions.
notes.plans: After g6, if White plays d4, Black proceeds with Bg7 and h3, transposing to known Gurgenidze theory. If White plays d3 (Breer), Black plays d5 and later e5, creating an active position.

notes.explains: In the Breer (d3) setup, Black plays d5 and then e5, avoiding the typical Caro-Kann pawn structure with a pawn on e6. This opens the bishop and gives Black active play.
notes.teaches: When White delays central occupation, Black can seize space with e5, leading to a freer game.
notes.plans: After e5, Black develops with Nf3, Bd6, and castles, fighting for the center and the e-file.

notes.explains: In the Exchange Caro-Kann, Black plays g6 to prevent White's typical kingside attack, especially targeting the weak h7 square. This leads to a plan with Nh6, Nf5, and Nd6, controlling key squares.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like g6 can neutralize an opponent's attacking plans and create a solid but active setup.
notes.plans: Black castles, plays Kh8 to avoid the diagonal, and maneuvers the knight to d6, while preparing f6 and e5 if possible. If White challenges the knight with Nb5, Black retreats to e8 to maintain control.

notes.explains: In the Accelerated Panov, after White plays c4, Black can deviate from the usual Nf6 and e6 or c6 by taking on c4 immediately. This rare move is not unsound; it is equal according to the engine. The idea is to follow up with Qc7, putting pressure on both bishops.
notes.teaches: When facing a well-known line, a rare but sound move can be a practical weapon because your opponent is unlikely to know the best response.
notes.plans: After White recaptures, play Qc7 to pressure the bishops. If White retreats the bishop to b3, play Bg4 to provoke f3, then retreat the bishop to d7. Aim to blockade the d-pawn and play against it as a static weakness.

notes.explains: After Qc7 and Bb3, Black plays Bg4. White must respond with f3, as other moves allow Black to take on c1 and win the bishop pair or gain a comfortable position. This provokes two weaknesses in White's camp.
notes.teaches: Provoking pawn moves like f3 can create permanent weaknesses in the opponent's structure, especially if they are not compensated by activity.
notes.plans: After f3, retreat the bishop to d7. Continue developing and aim to set up a blockade on the d-pawn. If White plays carelessly, such as castling and Bc2, play Nc6 and prepare Nb4-d5 to cement the blockade.

notes.explains: In the Accelerated Panov, instead of the normal Caro-Kann move d5, Black can transpose to the Old Indian with e5 and d6. This is not the most theoretically optimal, but it is a practical choice because the opponent is unlikely to know it well.
notes.teaches: Choosing a less common but sound opening can be a practical advantage, especially if you are more familiar with it than your opponent.
notes.plans: Play e5 and d6, and follow the Old Indian setup. If you prefer, you can play the normal Accelerated Panov, but the Old Indian is recommended for practical reasons.

notes.explains: Against the Goldman variation with Qf3, Black can exchange on e4 with Nxe4, then play Nf6. This rare move leads to a structure resembling the H3 Gorgan. If White doesn't take, Black can exchange and offer a queen trade with Qd5.
notes.teaches: In unfamiliar variations, a rare but sound move can steer the game into structures you know well, even if it deviates from the main lines.
notes.plans: After Nxe4 and Nf6, if White plays c3, exchange on e4 and play Qd5, offering a queen trade. This leads to a comfortable structure for Black.

notes.explains: In closed center positions, the central pawns are locked and both the d- and e-files are blocked, so rooks have little scope and bishops are often restricted by their own pawns. This reduces the practical value of rooks and bishops, while knights become relatively more powerful because they can jump over the pawn wall.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, prioritize knights over bishops and rooks; they are typically the most valuable pieces until the center opens.

notes.explains: In a locked pawn center, one side usually has a pawn advanced beyond the fourth rank, giving that side more space. For example, an advanced pawn on e5 controls d6 and f6, restricting the opponent's pieces.
notes.teaches: Recognize which side has more space in closed positions; the side with more space should keep minor pieces on the board, while the side with less space should trade them off.

notes.explains: In the French Defense, after the typical c5 break, the center can become blocked, leading to a closed structure. The c5 break is a key way for Black to challenge White's pawn chain and create counterplay.
notes.teaches: In closed openings like the French, the c5 pawn break is a standard method for Black to undermine White's center and open the position.
notes.plans: After c5 and the subsequent exchanges, both sides should reposition their pieces for the resulting closed or semi-closed structure.

notes.explains: In closed positions, the side with less space (often Black) should aim to trade pieces, especially minor pieces, to reduce the opponent's space advantage and exploit structural weaknesses like doubled pawns.
notes.teaches: When you have less space, simplify the position. Trade off pieces to give your remaining pieces more room and to highlight any pawn weaknesses in the opponent's camp.
notes.plans: If you are Black in a closed King's Indian structure, look for trades and breaks like a5 or f5 to create counterplay.

notes.explains: In the example from the Nimzo-Indian, after the center closes, Black has a knight versus bishop imbalance. The knight can be more valuable in closed positions because it can maneuver around the blocked pawns, while the bishop is limited by them.
notes.teaches: In closed centers, knights often outperform bishops because they can hop over pawns. Use your knight to target weaknesses like the f4 square, and provoke pawn moves that create further weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black can play moves like ...Nh4 to pressure f4, ...a5 to gain space, and ...Qa5 to attack the queenside, while keeping the center closed.

notes.explains: In closed center positions, grabbing space on the wings is crucial, but direct attacking chances are rare. The game often revolves around maneuvering and improving piece placement rather than immediate tactics.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, prioritize space gains and piece activity over speculative attacks. Look for long-term plans like expanding on the flank or preparing a timely pawn break.
notes.plans: Both sides should seek to maximize their space and piece activity, while waiting for the right moment to open the position with a pawn break.

notes.explains: In closed center positions, the center is locked, so bishops lack diagonals, knights lack outposts, and rooks are inactive. The queens are often the only active pieces, as seen when the queen made several moves to pressure a weakness.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, prioritize gaining space and be patient, as tactical opportunities are rare. Maneuver pieces to slowly improve their activity.
notes.plans: Look for pawn breaks to open lines and create outposts for your pieces.

notes.explains: When the center is completely locked, a knight on e8 can be better than a bishop on c1 because the knight has potential to reach strong outposts, while the bishop is blocked by its own pawns.
notes.teaches: Piece quality matters more than nominal value in closed positions; a 'bad' bishop can be a permanent weakness, while a knight can be rerouted to a good square.
notes.plans: Reroute the knight to a better square, such as f5 or d5, and use pawn breaks to open lines for the bishop.

notes.explains: When your opponent has a pawn break coming, you can often march your king away to safety because the closed center gives you time. This was done by moving the king to the other side of the board.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, you have time to improve your king's safety before the position opens up. Use that time to move your king away from the side where the pawn break will occur.
notes.plans: Identify the likely pawn break and move your king to the opposite wing.

notes.explains: When your opponent has a pawn break, the most common reaction is to defend the recapture square with a pawn, giving the opponent the least activity. This was done by defending h3 so that if h5 is played, the pawn can recapture.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn break, consider defending the recapture square to minimize your opponent's piece activity after the exchange.
notes.plans: Prepare to meet the pawn break by reinforcing the recapture square.

notes.explains: In closed positions, you must prevent your opponent from infiltrating with a rook on the seventh rank, as that can be decisive. Here, the rook reached h2, creating serious threats.
notes.teaches: Control the seventh rank and prevent enemy rook infiltration, especially in closed positions where other pieces are inactive.
notes.plans: Keep rooks active on the seventh rank and use them to create threats, while preventing your opponent from doing the same.

notes.explains: In this closed center position, White's bishops are dead pieces, while Black's knight is far superior. The infiltration on the second rank with the rook has made Black's position virtually winning.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, a knight can be much stronger than a bishop, especially if the bishops are blocked by their own pawns. Trading pieces when you have the superior minor piece is a winning strategy.
notes.plans: Black should continue to trade pieces and target White's weaknesses, such as the doubled pawns and the c4 pawn, while keeping the knight active.

notes.explains: The game was won because Black had a knight versus a bishop, and the position was closed. If the knight were exchanged for the bishop, the position would be a dead draw.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, knights are often better than bishops because they can jump over pawns and find strong outposts. Always consider the relative value of minor pieces in the specific pawn structure.

notes.explains: The lesson from this game is that in closed center positions, you must find the pawn break to open lines for your pieces. Here, h5 was the key break that allowed infiltration.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, look for pawn breaks on the flanks to create weaknesses and open files for your rooks. Stopping your opponent's counterplay is also crucial.

notes.explains: In another closed center position (King's Indian, closed variation), White launched a kingside attack with g4, h4, h5, while Black's counterplay on the queenside was insufficient. The attack was overwhelming.
notes.teaches: If the center is closed, you can often attack on the flank where you have space, while your opponent's counterplay on the other side is too slow. Marching your pawns up the board can create a decisive attack.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack, bringing more pieces to the kingside, while keeping the king safe. Black must find active counterplay to distract White.

notes.explains: White made a mistake by moving the knight from f3 to e2, which removed a defender of the d5 pawn and allowed a tactical sacrifice. The engine evaluation dropped from +2 to -0.7.
notes.teaches: When attacking, do not move pieces away from key defensive duties unless necessary. Even in a winning attack, one inaccuracy can turn the tables.
notes.plans: White should have kept the knight on f3 to maintain the attack and defend d5. Instead, after the mistake, Black gets counterplay.

notes.explains: When the opponent leaves their king in the center and launches an attack, the defender often has a chance to counter by opening the center. In this position, the center is closed, but the white king is exposed, so a sacrifice to break open the center can be decisive.
notes.teaches: If your opponent attacks while their king is still in the center, look for opportunities to open the center, even at the cost of material. A knight sacrifice on d5 can dissolve the closed center and expose the enemy king.
notes.plans: Consider moves like Nxd5, followed by exd5 and Rxb2, to open lines and activate all your pieces against the exposed king.

notes.explains: In closed center positions, pieces can become passive, especially knights on poor squares. Here, the knight on g3 is not contributing, and the rook on b8 and bishop on b2 are well placed, but the center is still closed.
notes.teaches: Always look for potential sacrifices in closed centers, especially with knights. A knight on a useless square can be sacrificed to open the position and create attacking chances.
notes.plans: If the center is closed and your opponent's king is exposed, seek a pawn break or piece sacrifice to open lines. For example, a knight on d5 can be sacrificed to break open the center.

notes.explains: In a closed center, the side with more space should avoid unnecessary piece trades because the opponent's pieces are cramped and lack coordination. Trading helps the defender free their position.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage in a closed position, keep pieces on the board to maintain pressure and restrict the opponent's activity.
notes.plans: Continue expanding on the side where you have space, while keeping the center closed and avoiding trades that relieve the opponent's congestion.

notes.explains: With a space advantage, further pawn advances can restrict the opponent's pieces even more, taking away squares from their knights, bishops, and queen. This can create outposts for your own pieces.
notes.teaches: If you have space, try to gain even more space by advancing pawns, but do so carefully to avoid creating weaknesses. Use pawns to control key squares and limit the opponent's piece mobility.
notes.plans: Look for pawn breaks that expand your space and create outposts, while ensuring the center remains closed to your advantage.

notes.explains: The opponent's only counterplay might be a specific pawn break. By over-defending the square where that break would occur, you can completely neutralize their plan and leave them without any active ideas.
notes.teaches: Identify the opponent's potential pawn breaks and prevent them by placing multiple defenders on the key squares, suffocating their counterplay.
notes.plans: Keep reinforcing the critical squares, and if the opponent tries the break anyway, you can win material or maintain a dominant position.

notes.explains: In a closed position with a space advantage, a knight can become extremely powerful, especially if it lands on a strong outpost. Conversely, a bad bishop can be traded off for a good knight, leaving you with a superior minor piece.
notes.teaches: Use your space advantage to create strong outposts for your knights. Trade off your bad pieces for the opponent's good ones, and avoid trading your active pieces for their passive ones.
notes.plans: Place your knight on a dominant square, trade off your bad bishop for the opponent's good knight, and then exploit the resulting piece superiority.

notes.explains: In closed center positions, the side with more space should follow a clear strategy: keep the center closed, avoid piece trades, expand with pawns, and look for pawn breaks that open the position to your own advantage.
notes.teaches: A closed center favors the side with more space. Use that space to restrict the opponent, improve your pieces, and only open the position when it benefits you.
notes.plans: Apply these principles: maintain the closed center, expand on the side where you have space, and prepare breaks that create weaknesses in the opponent's camp.

notes.explains: The Jobava London is a setup opening for White, starting with d4 and Nc3, followed by Bf4. Black's responses determine the setup, and the most common are d5, Nf6, g6, or c5. If Black avoids d5, White can consider playing e4 to transpose into Pirc or Modern setups.
notes.teaches: In setup openings, White's moves are flexible and aim to create attacking chances regardless of Black's setup. Recognizing Black's main options helps White choose the most principled continuation.
notes.plans: After d4, Nc3, and Bf4, White prepares to castle queenside and pressure c7. If Black plays d5, White continues with e3 and Qd2, maintaining the setup.

notes.explains: The moves Nc3 and Bf4 serve two purposes: they enable White to castle queenside quickly (after moving the queen), and they put pressure on c7. A common attacking theme is Nb5, hitting c7, which can be strong if Black neglects a6.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, White's development is geared toward a quick queenside attack. The knight on c3 and bishop on f4 coordinate to target Black's queenside weaknesses.
notes.plans: White aims to play Qd2, castle queenside, and then consider Nb5 to pressure c7. Black often responds with a6 to prevent Nb5.

notes.explains: The Jobava London is an aggressive, rare opening with straightforward attacking ideas. It is not divided into heavy theoretical variations like other openings; instead, White follows a setup and adapts to Black's choices.
notes.teaches: Learning a setup opening can be more about understanding ideas and typical plans than memorizing long variations. Practicing against a human-like opponent helps internalize these patterns.
notes.plans: White's setup involves d4, Nc3, Bf4, e3, and Qd2, with the option to castle queenside and launch an attack. Black's main defensive move is a6 to prevent Nb5.

notes.explains: In the Jobava London, white often delays queenside castling and avoids the c-pawn break, instead focusing on immediate pressure against c7 with moves like Nb5. Black's typical response is a6 to prevent this.
notes.teaches: A recurring attacking theme in this system is Nb5, targeting the c7 pawn. If black doesn't play a6 promptly, Nb5 becomes a strong option.
notes.plans: After a6, continue with e3, Qd2, and queenside castling, preparing to attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black's main setup involves d5, g6, and Nf6, often with a6. White can punish the immediate g6 by opening the queen's diagonal with e3, developing the bishop to d3 or e2, and aiming for Ne5 to pressure black early.
notes.teaches: When black plays g6 early, white should quickly develop with e3 and prepare Ne5, putting pressure on black's position before they can consolidate.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to d3 or e2, play Ne5, and consider h4 to start a kingside attack.

notes.explains: A key downside of the Jobava London is that the c-pawn is blocked, meaning white can never support d4 with c3 nor break black's center with c4. This leaves white's center vulnerable to c5 by black, while black's center remains solid.
notes.teaches: When playing Nc3 in this system, you must be aware that your center can be undermined, but you cannot undermine black's. Good players compensate with aggressive moves like h4 to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: Use the kingside attack to compensate for the central weaknesses, often with h4-h5 to open lines.

notes.explains: In the model game, white sacrifices material (exchange) to maintain a powerful attacking position. All white's pieces coordinate against black's king, while black's rooks are passive and ineffective.
notes.teaches: In sharp attacking positions, material can be irrelevant if the opponent's pieces are undeveloped and your own pieces work together. Focus on piece activity and king safety over material.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with moves like Qh2 pressuring c7, then Bc7 to win material or force weaknesses, and use the h-file for the rook.

notes.explains: White's plan is to break down black's kingside structure with f4 and g5, opening lines for the pieces. Even after giving up the exchange, white's pieces are all active and black's are tied down.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and attacking chances, look for pawn breaks like f4 and g5 to open the position and increase the pressure. Sacrifices are justified if they accelerate the attack.
notes.plans: Play f4 and g5 to break open the kingside, then use the open files and diagonals to deliver mate or win material.

notes.explains: In this aggressive system, White fights for two things: the c7 square and a kingside attack, achieved by opening up all the pieces. The main setup involves knight f6, g6, and d5 from Black, which occurs most of the time.
notes.teaches: Identify the primary targets in a position—here, c7 and the enemy king—and orient your piece play toward them.
notes.plans: Develop pieces harmoniously, aiming to create threats on both the queenside and kingside.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Bf4 d5 e3 Bg7, playing Nb5 early is not valuable because Black can chase it back with ...a6, wasting White's time. However, in setups where Black plays ...e6 instead of ...g6, Nb5 is a good idea.
notes.teaches: Don't commit a knight to an outpost if it can be easily driven back; reserve such moves for when they are truly effective.
notes.plans: In the g6-d5 setup, continue with h4 to start the kingside attack.

notes.explains: After the main setup, White plays h4. Black's best response is h5 to prevent White from advancing further. If Black plays Bg4 instead, White can play f3, gaining a tempo and then continue with g4 anyway.
notes.teaches: When launching a pawn storm, be ready to meet defensive moves with tempo-gaining responses that maintain your initiative.
notes.plans: If Black plays h5, switch to a plan with Qd2, O-O-O, Nf3, aiming for Ne5. If Black plays Bg4, allow the trade and then play for e4.

notes.explains: Black's main strategic goal in the Benoni is to trade off the light-squared bishop, which is actually their good bishop. White invites this trade because White's bishop is the bad one, so playing Bb5+ and after Bd7, a4 prevents Black from ever playing b5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's beneficial to trade off a bishop that appears good for the opponent, especially if it's your bad bishop. Prophylactic moves like a4 can stop key pawn breaks.
notes.plans: After a4, continue development with Nf3, castle, and prepare e5.

notes.explains: The knight on f3 is essential because White wants to play e5. If Black trades it off with Bg4, White's e5 plan is compromised, and Black can later challenge with Ne5, leaving White's center insecure.
notes.teaches: Don't allow trades that cripple your central pawn breaks. Sometimes a knight is more valuable than a bishop pair, especially when it supports a key pawn advance.
notes.plans: Prevent Bg4 by playing h3 or Nbd2, then castle and prepare e5 with Re1.

notes.explains: After the bishop trade, White can choose between Nbd2, h3, or castling. Nbd2 is preferred because it never allows the trade and supports a plan with Rd1 pressuring d6. Alternatively, h3 allows a normal Benoni setup with Re1 and e5.
notes.teaches: There are multiple viable plans; choose based on your style. Nbd2 gives control over e5 and pressure on d6, while h3 is more standard.
notes.plans: If Nbd2, play Rd1 and target d6. If h3, castle kingside, play Re1, and aim for e5.

notes.explains: In the setup with d5 and c5, if Black doesn't play a6, White can play Nb5 immediately after e6. This forces ...Na6 to defend c7, and the knight can later go to the queenside. If Black plays c5 first, Nb5 is less effective due to Qa5+, so White plays e3 first.
notes.teaches: Use tactical motifs like Nb5 to exploit weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure. Timing is crucial: play Nb5 when it's most effective, and consider checks like Qa5+ that can refute premature moves.
notes.plans: After Nb5 and ...Na6, play e3, Nf3, and castle. If Black plays c5, play e3 first to prepare Nb5.

notes.explains: In this line, black's knight on a6 is forced to defend c7. White plays e3 to prepare knight b5, which would target c7 and a6. If black plays c5 without a6, knight b5 is met by queen a5 check, so white first plays e3.
notes.teaches: When a knight is attacking a weak pawn, sometimes you need to prepare the jump with a move that prevents a check or other resource, rather than playing it immediately.
notes.plans: After e3, if black plays c5, white can consider exchanging on d4 or playing knight b5 if black doesn't play a6. The knight on b5 prevents a6 and keeps control of c7.

notes.explains: If black plays c5 without a6, white can exchange on d4, leading to a structure where white has a 'cow's butt' pawn structure (c3, d4, e3) and the knight is on c3 instead of d2. This is a normal but slightly awkward London setup.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you get a playable but not ideal structure; the key is to know how to handle it: move the knight to e2, play c3, and aim for the e5 square.
notes.plans: Develop with knight f3, bishop e2, then reposition the knight to e2 and prepare c3, playing for e5.

notes.explains: When black plays d5 and c5 with a6, white's knight cannot go to b5, so the game takes a different path. Black often plays e6 to challenge the f4 bishop, but c5 without e6 can be a pawn sacrifice.
notes.teaches: In some openings, a pawn sacrifice can be dangerous for the defender if they cannot regain the pawn without compromising their position (e.g., giving up the dark-squared bishop).
notes.plans: If black plays c5 without e6, white can capture on c5 and then play b4, maintaining the extra pawn. If black plays e6 first, white should be prepared for a slow, positional game.

notes.explains: In the Jobava London, black can adopt a slow, solid setup that aims to neutralize white's play and draw the game. This setup leaves black with a bad bishop, but white must find a way to create imbalance.
notes.teaches: When facing a solid, passive setup, look for a pawn thrust like g4 to create kingside chances and unbalance the position, even if it seems risky.
notes.plans: After g4, if black plays Bc5, continue with g5, forcing the knight back, then Nf3, discouraging black from castling kingside. White's flexible bishop can later be traded or used actively.

notes.explains: Against another slow setup with e6 and Be7, white should immediately play Nb5, forcing black's knight to a6, which is a slight concession. White then builds up on the kingside with moves like Nf3, h4, and later c3 to support the center.
notes.teaches: When black delays c5, a knight sortie to b5 can provoke weaknesses or force black's pieces to awkward squares, gaining time for your own development.
notes.plans: Continue with kingside expansion: Qc1, Bd3, Ng5 or Ne5, aiming to pressure h7 and keep pushing pawns. Black's f6 would create a hook for the g-pawn, so white maintains control of e5.

notes.explains: When black plays Bf5 early, white should switch plans entirely and play f3, then e4, establishing a strong center. This avoids the typical Jobava London setup and transposes to an English Attack-like formation with the bishop on e3 instead of f4.
notes.teaches: If the opponent plays a provocative move like Bf5, be ready to change your plan and seize the center with f3 and e4, supporting it with the bishop on e3.
notes.plans: After e4, if black plays Bb4, ignore it and play h4 to trap the bishop on g6. Then proceed with Qd2, g4, f4, and g5, building a crushing kingside attack if black castles short.

notes.explains: In the Jobava London, when Black develops the bishop to b4, White can ignore it and focus on a kingside pawn storm with h4, g4, f4, and g5, aiming to crush Black if they castle kingside.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best response to a pin or a developing move is to ignore it and pursue your own aggressive plan, especially if the opponent's piece is not immediately threatening.
notes.plans: Continue the pawn storm on the kingside, bringing the queen to d2 to support the advance.

notes.explains: Against a King's Indian setup (Black avoids d5 and builds a KID structure), White can play h4, Qd2, castle queenside, and then advance d5. This move gives the knight access to d4 and misplaces the c6 knight, which often has to retreat and block the bishop.
notes.teaches: A central pawn break like d5 can serve dual purposes: creating a strong outpost for a knight and forcing the opponent's piece to a passive square.
notes.plans: After d5, if the knight retreats to a7, White can continue with natural moves like Nf3 and Nd4, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Against the Dutch (f5), the Jobava setup is not appropriate; instead, White should play Nc3 and then Bg5, not Bf4, because Bf4 allows d6 and e5, giving Black a good game.
notes.teaches: Opening systems are not universal; you must adapt your setup based on your opponent's first moves, choosing the most principled development.
notes.plans: In the Dutch, develop normally with Nc3 and Bg5, avoiding the Jobava setup.

notes.explains: In the Miles Variation, Black's typical light-square strategies like Ba6 are less effective because White's bishop is already on f4, so e3 is a natural and strong response, not an awkward concession. The bishop is not blocked, and White's position remains harmonious.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a move like Ba6, consider whether it forces a real weakness or just a natural developing move. If the opponent's response is comfortable, the move loses its point.
notes.plans: Black should instead consider main lines like Be7 or Bb4+ to create counterplay. White can proceed with e3 and Nf3, maintaining a solid structure.

notes.explains: The Miles Variation is not objectively best for White; Black can often equalize or even get a slight edge. However, it is a practical choice because many Black players are unfamiliar with the resulting positions, which resemble a London System with c4 already played.
notes.teaches: Practical opening choices can be effective even if they are not theoretically critical. Familiarity with the resulting structures is a key advantage.
notes.plans: Black should aim to challenge the center with c5 or b6 and develop pieces actively. White should focus on rapid development and maintaining a flexible pawn structure.

notes.explains: Against the Dutch, black's f5 controls e4, but if white avoids d4 and plays d3, black's main idea is blunted. White's setup with g3, Bg2, Nc3, and d3-e4 puts pressure on light squares and fights for e4.
notes.teaches: When facing the Dutch, consider delaying d4 and instead play d3 to maintain control of e4, then challenge with e4. This undermines black's typical Dutch plans.
notes.plans: Develop with g3, Bg2, Nc3, and prepare e4. If black plays ...e5, look for opportune moments to play d4 later.

notes.explains: Against the Leningrad Dutch, black will likely play g6, Bg7, d6, and later f5. White's plan is to use the same setup with e4, transposing to a King's Indian-like position with an early f5.
notes.teaches: Against the Leningrad, maintain the flexible setup and aim for e4 to challenge black's center. The bishop on g2 will be powerful on the long diagonal.
notes.plans: Play g3, Bg2, Nc3, d3, and prepare e4. If black castles and plays f5, continue with e4 to open the center.

notes.explains: The classical Dutch is not good for black because white can storm the queenside and gain space, while the light-squared bishop becomes very strong. The downside of d3 is allowing ...e5, but white can later play d4 to punish it.
notes.teaches: Against the classical Dutch, focus on queenside expansion and use the bishop on g2 to pressure black's light squares. Be ready to play d4 later to challenge black's center.
notes.plans: Develop with g3, Bg2, Nc3, and d3. Then expand on the queenside with b4 and c5, and consider d4 when appropriate.

notes.explains: The Stonewall is the best defense for black. Black aims to control e4 with pawns on d5 and f5. White should avoid setups like Nc3, Nf3, and e3, and instead play d3, g3, Bg2 to control e4 and prepare e4 to break the wall.
notes.teaches: Against the Stonewall, use a setup with g3, Bg2, and d3 to control e4, then break with e4. This challenges black's central pawn chain.
notes.plans: Play g3, Bg2, Nf3, and d3. Castle, then prepare e4. If black plays ...dxe4, recapture and continue development with Nc3.

notes.explains: In the Stonewall, black must build the wall (d5 and f5) before developing bishops. If black plays ...Be7 or ...Bd6 early, white can take on d5 and leave black with weaknesses. After ...cxd5, white plays Nc3, and black's position is worse.
notes.teaches: Punish early bishop development in the Stonewall by capturing on d5. This leaves black with a weak e6 pawn and a bad bishop, while white has a solid center and active pieces.
notes.plans: After ...dxc5, play Nc3 and develop. Use the c-file and the bishop pair to pressure black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: After White plays Nc3 and d3, Black's d5-pawn weaknesses are not easily punished, so Black should castle. White has the c-file and strong bishops, making the position comfortable for White.
notes.teaches: In the Stonewall setup, White can play d3 instead of d4 to avoid giving Black dynamic chances. The c-file and bishop pair are long-term assets.
notes.plans: White can continue with e4, aiming to occupy e5, or play b3 with a fianchetto, but the e4 plan is preferred.

notes.explains: If Black plays d4 early, White can simply take on d4. Against Be7, after cxd4 Nc3, if Black plays d4, White has Qa4+ winning the pawn. Thus Black must play c6 before developing the bishop.
notes.teaches: In these structures, a premature d4 by Black can be met by tactics like Qa4+ to punish the pawn push. Black's move order matters to avoid such tactics.
notes.plans: White should be ready to meet d4 with cxd4 and then exploit the pin or check.

notes.explains: After Black castles and White plays e4, Black must react to the threat of occupying e5. If Black ignores it, White can take on f5, play Re1, and Bf4, dominating e5 and crushing Black positionally.
notes.teaches: The e4 push in the Stonewall is not just a pawn move; it's a strategic bid to control e5. If Black allows it, White gets a bind on the key square.
notes.plans: White's plan is to occupy e5 with pieces, restricting Black's bishop and pieces.

notes.explains: If Black plays d4 in the position after Nc3, White can play Na4 in Benoni style. This move is strong, and if Black plays b5, it fails to cxb5 cxb5 Ne5. If Black plays c5, White can play a3 and b4, sacrificing a pawn for a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: In the reversed Benoni, White can use the knight maneuver Na4 to target the d4 pawn and create play. The pawn sacrifice with b4 is a dynamic way to open lines.
notes.plans: After Na4, if Black plays c5, White plays a3 and b4, and if the pawn is taken, White gets active play with the knight and bishops.

notes.explains: In the English Opening, White's e4 push aims to occupy e5, creating a bind that restricts Black's pieces, especially the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: A central pawn advance can be used to gain a space advantage and restrict the opponent's piece activity, even if it seems counterintuitive.
notes.plans: Follow up with Rook e1 and Bishop f4 to reinforce the e5 outpost and maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Against e4, Black has critical responses: d4 or f4. If Black plays a passive move like a6, White can take on f5, then play Rook e1 and Bishop f4, dominating e5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent ignores a central threat, punish them by strengthening your grip on key central squares.
notes.plans: After f5 is captured, continue with Rook e1 and Bishop f4 to maintain the bind.

notes.explains: If Black plays d4, White can respond with Knight e2, and if f4 then d4, the pawn on d4 cannot be captured due to tactics (Knight takes d4). The engine gives White a large advantage, though it may be exaggerated.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn offer is poisoned; capturing it leads to a worse position. Recognize such tactical motifs.
notes.plans: Develop pieces harmoniously, aiming for control of key squares like e5 and d5.

notes.explains: If Black plays f4, White takes with the pawn. If Black recaptures with e4, White can play Knight g5, winning the pawn back and leaving Black with weaknesses. If Black plays d takes c4, it's not wise to grab the pawn; instead, White should focus on central control.
notes.teaches: In such positions, prioritize central control over material gains. Use tactics to regain pawns while maintaining a positional bind.
notes.plans: Aim to place knights on d4 and e4, restricting Black's piece mobility.

notes.explains: Against the Classical Dutch, if Black plays c6, White can strike with e4 immediately, aiming for a bind on d5. If Black plays Knight c6, White can attack on the queenside with Rook b1 and pawn advances.
notes.teaches: Different responses require different plans: central strike vs. flank attack. Adapt your strategy based on the opponent's setup.
notes.plans: For c6, play e4, then f4, d4, and e5 to gain a bind. For Knight c6, play Rook b1 and prepare b4, a4, etc.

notes.explains: If Black plays e5 in the Classical Dutch, White can immediately play b4, starting a queenside attack. If Black continues with Queen e8, White plays a4, and Black must prevent further advances.
notes.teaches: When the opponent commits to a kingside plan, counter on the queenside with pawn storms, gaining space and creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: Continue with a4, b4, and possibly a5, aiming to open lines and create passed pawns.

notes.explains: In the Classical Dutch against the English, White can achieve a huge advantage with a strong space advantage and a powerful diagonal, leading to many weaknesses in Black's camp. The engine evaluation is very high for White.
notes.teaches: When facing the Classical Dutch, White should focus on gaining space and exploiting the weakened dark squares, often by advancing pawns and developing the bishop to a strong diagonal.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...e5, White can immediately play b4, and if Black plays ...Qe8, White can play a4, followed by Ba3, preparing to break down Black's structure.

notes.explains: The Leningrad Dutch often transposes to King's Indian-type positions where Black plays an early ...f5. White should aim for a setup with d3, e4, and a fianchettoed bishop, avoiding an early Nf3.
notes.teaches: Against the Leningrad, White can adopt a King's Indian-like setup, controlling the light squares and preparing to challenge the center with e4.
notes.plans: Develop with Nc3, Bg2, and e4, then decide based on Black's responses (whether they take on e4 or play ...d6).

notes.explains: In the Leningrad, after White plays e4, Black has the option to take on e4 or not. If Black plays ...c6, White should capture on f5 to prepare d4, aiming to fix Black's pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When Black plays ...c6 in these structures, it's a signal to take on f5 and then play d4, creating a strong pawn center and targeting Black's weaknesses.
notes.plans: After ...c6, take on f5, then play d4. If Black recaptures with the pawn, continue with d4, and if Black plays ...Na6, solidify with b3 and prepare Bg5 and d5.

notes.explains: If Black does not take on e4 and instead plays ...d6, ...c6, and ...e5, White should still take on f5 when ...c6 appears, and then aim for Bg5 and d5 to cement a pawn on d5 and create a target on d6.
notes.teaches: The plan is to fix Black's pawns in the center so they become permanent weaknesses that can be attacked later.
notes.plans: Play d4, then if Black plays ...Na6, continue with Bg5 and d5, regardless of whether Black recaptures with the bishop or pawn on f5.

notes.explains: Against the Dutch, White can aim to trade the d-pawn for Black's f-pawn, leaving Black with a weak d6 pawn and giving White a space advantage. If Black avoids the trade and plays d6, c6, and e5, White can still target the center with moves like Bg5 and d5.
notes.teaches: When facing the Dutch, consider trading your d-pawn for Black's f-pawn to create a lasting weakness on d6 and gain space.
notes.plans: If Black takes on e4, recapture with the pawn and proceed with the standard Benoni setup. If Black declines, play Bg5 and d5 to fix the center.

notes.explains: In the Benoni, the symmetrical pawn structure gives both sides pawn breaks. Black no longer has ...f5 because the f-pawn is gone, but White has f4, and both sides have b5/b4 breaks. The d5 square is a great outpost for a knight.
notes.teaches: In symmetrical Benoni structures, remember the thematic pawn breaks and that occupying d5 with a knight is almost always good.
notes.plans: Play f4 immediately if possible, and consider Nd5 if Black attacks the pawn.

notes.explains: If Black captures on f4, White should recapture with the bishop to put pressure on d6, rather than with the pawn, which is riskier. The engine prefers the bishop recapture.
notes.teaches: When recapturing on f4 in this Benoni, prefer the bishop to maintain pressure and avoid weakening your structure.
notes.plans: After Bxf4, continue to target d6 and ask questions of Black's position.

notes.explains: Against different Dutch setups, White adapts: against the Stonewall, use the Benoni with a knight on f3; against the Classical, claim space on the queenside with b4, a4, and b5.
notes.teaches: Tailor your plan against the Dutch based on Black's specific setup: Benoni for fianchetto, knight on f3 for Stonewall, queenside expansion for Classical.
notes.plans: Choose the appropriate setup and proceed with the corresponding plan.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In the closed Ruy Lopez, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7, the move Re1 attacks the e5 pawn indirectly. If Black plays …b5 and White retreats Bb3, Black has a choice: the solid …d6 or the immediate …O-O, which invites the Marshall Gambit after c3 d5.
notes.teaches: The Marshall Gambit is a pawn sacrifice for long-term attacking chances: Black gives up a pawn to get rapid development, open lines, and pressure against the white king. White must decide whether to accept the gambit or avoid it with anti-Marshall moves.
notes.plans: If Black plays the Marshall, White can either accept the pawn with exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5, or decline with moves like d4 or a4 to steer into other lines.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In the Marshall Gambit, after …d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5, Black has compensation: the white queenside is undeveloped, the bishops aim at the kingside, and the queen can go to h4. The move …c6 defends the knight, and …d4 opens lines for the bishop.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing a pawn, the compensation must be active: lead in development, open lines, and create immediate threats. Here Black's pieces coordinate against the white king, making the pawn sacrifice sound.
notes.plans: Black continues with ...Bd6, ...Re8, and ...Qh4, building up an attack. White must defend accurately to survive the onslaught.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: White can avoid the Marshall by playing d4, the Yates variation. This move prevents Black's ...d5 break and instead invites a different type of game. Black can respond with …Nxd4, which is uncommon, or …d6, transposing to the main line of the Yates.
notes.teaches: Anti-Marshall lines aim to sidestep Black's prepared attack. By playing d4, White changes the character of the position, but must be ready for Black's alternative setups.
notes.plans: If Black plays …Nxd4, White can recapture and possibly try Bxf7+ to exploit the loose knight. More commonly, Black plays …d6, and after c3, the game enters the Yates main line with ...Bg4.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In the Yates variation, after d4 d6 c3, Black often plays …Bg4, pinning the knight. White's main response is Be3, and then Black can play ...Nxd4, ...c5, or other moves to create counterplay.
notes.teaches: The Yates variation avoids h3, allowing Black to pin the knight with ...Bg4. This pin can be annoying, but White can develop harmoniously and aim for central control.
notes.plans: Black may play ...Nxd4, ...c5, or ...Qd7 to pressure the center. White should aim to consolidate and exploit the pin if Black overextends.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez Exchange variation, after White plays d4 early, Black's knight on c6 can become a liability if it goes to a5 at the wrong time. The position is closed, and White can restrict the knight, making it useless.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a knight on the rim can be permanently sidelined if the opponent can control the key squares. Always consider whether your knight's outpost is stable before committing it.
notes.plans: If Black wants to play ...Na5, ensure that ...c5 can follow quickly to challenge the center, or else the knight will be trapped.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: After Black played ...Na5 and ...c5, White has a strong idea: push d4-d5, closing the center and completely cutting off the knight's retreat squares. The knight on a5 has no future, as ...Nb7 is slow and can be met by c4, and ...Nc4 is met by Bxc4, ruining Black's pawns.
notes.teaches: When an enemy knight is on the rim, a central pawn push can permanently imprison it. This is a common strategic motif: use pawns to restrict minor pieces.
notes.plans: White should play d5, then follow up with c4 to prevent any knight maneuver back into the game. Black's knight is effectively out of play.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In the same variation, Black's correct plan is to liquidate the center with ...dxc4, then play ...c5, challenging White's center. This gives the knight a safe retreat to c6 or allows ...c4 to gain space, avoiding the trap of ...Na5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a central pawn duo, it's often wise to trade one pawn to reduce the tension and create counterplay. A knight on the rim is only good if it can be supported by pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Black should aim for ...c5 and ...c4, forcing White to deal with the passed pawn or trade pieces, giving Black active play.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In the game, Black played ...Bxf3 instead of retreating the bishop, which prevents White from playing d5 immediately. After Qxf3, White still has the option of d5, but Black has avoided the immediate crisis.
notes.teaches: Exchanging a bishop for a knight can be a way to relieve pressure and prevent a central pawn push. Sometimes giving up the bishop pair is worth it to maintain a solid structure.
notes.plans: Black should continue with ...Nd7 and ...f5, seeking kingside play, while White will try to exploit the bishop pair and the space advantage.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In this Ruy Lopez structure, the knight on a5 is misplaced and White should exploit it with d5, closing the center and leaving the knight out of play. If Black recaptures and the knight returns via c6, the punishment has been avoided.
notes.teaches: A knight on the rim is a long-term weakness; strike with a central pawn break before the opponent can redeploy it.
notes.plans: Play d5 to close the center, then use the space advantage to build a kingside attack.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: After the opponent's aggressive h5, White had a safe reply in Qe2, because the threat of d3 is not real. The d6 pawn can be regained later, and White's structure is superior.
notes.teaches: Do not overreact to a pawn push that attacks a piece if the attack can be ignored or met with a developing move that maintains the better structure.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, then regain the d6 pawn with Nb3, keeping a slight edge.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In the resulting position, Black has a tactical shot: Nh5 attacks the bishop and threatens to trap the queen. White's attempts to save the bishop lead to a trapped queen or loss of material.
notes.teaches: When a piece is overloaded, look for a knight fork or a pin that wins material; a queen can be trapped if it has no escape squares.
notes.plans: For Black: play Nh5, then f6 to drive the bishop, and g5 to trap the queen if it tries to stay.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: After the queen is trapped, Black's attack continues with Qf4, preparing either Bf6-g7 winning the queen or Bf6-e5 checkmating on h2. White's defensive moves are insufficient.
notes.teaches: When you have a material or positional advantage, keep the initiative by creating multiple threats; a queen can be used to support a mating net.
notes.plans: For Black: play Qf4, then Bf6, and if White defends, use the threats to force mate or win more material.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In the final phase, White's king is exposed and Black's queen and rook coordinate to deliver mate. White's only defenses are too slow or lose material.
notes.teaches: A king exposed to a queen and rook can be mated even with material still on the board; look for forcing checks and mate threats.
notes.plans: For Black: continue with Qh3, threatening Qh2 mate, and if White blocks with f4, capture on f4 and win.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: In this position, the attacking side has a decisive mating threat against the enemy king. The defender's only try to block the mate on h2 is to play f4, but this allows the attacker to capture on f4 with the rook, and if the queen recaptures, the queen is lost; if the rook recaptures, a queen check on g3 or e3 wins material.
notes.teaches: When you have a direct mating threat, look for ways to convert it into material gain if the opponent tries to defend. A single defensive move may create new tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays f4 to defend the mate, capture on f4 with the rook and then exploit the resulting pins or checks to win the queen or deliver mate.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: The attacker also has a backup plan: if the opponent defends with rook g1, the queen can deliver mate on h3; otherwise, the rook can come to f2 and mate on h2 or g2. This shows that the attack is robust and has multiple ways to break through.
notes.teaches: When conducting an attack, it is important to have multiple threats so that the opponent cannot easily parry all of them. Look for ways to create a web of mating threats.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by either playing rook f2 to threaten mate on h2 or g2, or if the opponent plays rook g1, deliver mate with queen h3.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
notes.explains: The game was strategically unsound, but the player still won because he outplayed his opponent tactically and punished the mistake. This shows that even a strategically flawed game can be won if you capitalize on tactical opportunities.
notes.teaches: Do not underestimate the importance of tactics. Even if your strategy is not perfect, you can still win by being alert to tactical chances and punishing your opponent's errors.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian, after d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O, White's bishop to d3 is a mistake because it is blocked by the light-squared pawns on e4 and c4, making it a passive piece. It also gives Black the opportunity to play Bg4, pinning the knight and putting pressure on White's position.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the light-squared bishop for White is often a problem piece because it is hemmed in by the central pawns. Developing it to d3 can be a positional error, as it does not participate actively and allows Black to gain a tempo with Bg4.
notes.plans: Black should consider playing Bg4 to pin the knight and increase pressure, while maintaining the flexible King's Indian setup.

notes.explains: When White retreats the bishop to e2, Black can capture on f3 and then play e5, establishing a strong center. The bishop on g7 is not great, but Black plans to play f5 anyway, so the bishop's limited scope is not a major issue. After d5, White's bishop on e2 is even worse, and White wants to trade it off, but Black can continue with the typical King's Indian plan of f5.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, Black often accepts a passive bishop on g7 because the plan is to attack on the kingside with f5, which opens lines for the bishop and rook. The bishop's apparent passivity is compensated by the dynamic pawn storm.
notes.plans: Black should proceed with the standard King's Indian plan: play e5, then f5, and prepare a kingside attack. The bishop on g7 will become active after the pawn breaks.

notes.explains: Instead of the immediate f5, Black could also consider Nd4, even though it may create a weakness on d4. After the critical variation where White captures on d4, Black recaptures with the pawn, and the pawn on d4 is defended by the queen and later by the knight on d7. This pawn becomes a nuisance for White, as it is hard to capture and restricts White's pieces.
notes.teaches: Sometimes creating a 'weakness' like an isolated pawn can be a strength if it is well-defended and restricts the opponent's pieces. A passed or advanced pawn can tie down enemy pieces and provide a base for your own pieces.
notes.plans: Black could play Nd4, and if White captures, recapture with the pawn, then defend it with Qd6 and Nd7. The pawn on d4 will be a permanent thorn in White's side, and Black can continue with f5 or other breaks.

notes.explains: In the double-edged King's Indian, both sides attack on opposite wings. White's f4 push is risky because it weakens the kingside and allows Black to gain tempo and strong squares, whereas f3 would have slowed Black's attack.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the choice between f3 and f4 is critical: f3 is solid, f4 is aggressive but can backfire if Black gets counterplay.
notes.plans: If White plays f4, Black should look to open the f-file and use the f5 square for a knight, while White should aim for queenside play.

notes.explains: In a critical variation, Black can force a draw by trading pieces and creating a perpetual check, because White's rook and bishop are hanging, limiting defensive options.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are hanging, you can often force a perpetual or at least avoid losing; recognize when a draw is the best outcome.
notes.plans: If White plays the critical knight g3, Black should trade rooks and aim for a perpetual check.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, the white queen on g2 or h2 is not available because the rook on a1 and the bishop are hanging. The correct defensive resource is to play Kh1, which should lead to a draw by perpetual check.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's queen is eyeing your king, check whether their queen is tied to defending other pieces. If so, you may be able to force a perpetual check.
notes.plans: Play Kh1 to escape the checks and aim for a perpetual if the attack cannot be stopped.

notes.explains: Instead of the drawing line, White played Bc2, which allowed Black to play Nd4, attacking the queen and the bishop. After Qd2, the knight is defended, and Black can simply take the c4 pawn, winning material.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes an inaccurate move, look for tactical blows that hit multiple targets at once, such as a knight fork on d4.
notes.plans: Take the c4 pawn and maintain the initiative, as Black's pieces are actively placed.

notes.explains: White's next move Qf2 was even worse, as it loses the bishop. Black can simply take the bishop with the rook, and after Qxf2, a knight check wins the queen.
notes.teaches: Always check for simple captures and checks that win material. A single move can turn a losing position into a winning one.
notes.plans: Execute the tactical sequence to win the queen and force resignation.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian, after f3 f5, White's best move is f4 to stop Black's attack. The engine also likes a4 or Bc1, but f4 is the normal way to maintain the center and prevent Black from gaining space.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, White often needs to play f4 to counter Black's pawn storm on the kingside. Timing is crucial: if White delays, Black's attack becomes too strong.
notes.plans: Play f4 to solidify the center and prepare to counter on the queenside.

notes.explains: After f4, Black's attack is too slow, and White is better. Fischer played h6, but the engine prefers Bh6, putting pressure on the bishop. If White takes, Black recaptures with check, and if White plays fxe4, Black has strong tactics.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, active piece play is often better than slow pawn moves. Pressure on the opponent's pieces can create tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Consider Bh6 to increase the pressure and maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: Black's position is pleasant with the c5 and e5 squares available, and Black is attacking b2. The engine evaluates it as equal, but Black's pieces are visually appealing.
notes.teaches: Even when the engine says equal, a position with active pieces and weak opponent pawns can be easier to play. Trust your strategic assessment.
notes.plans: Maintain the pressure on b2 and look for ways to improve piece activity.

notes.explains: Black considered taking on b2, but after Bd4 and Kf1, the bishop would be needed for defense. Playing b6 is safer, as winning the pawn with g4 would lose a piece.
notes.teaches: Before grabbing a pawn, check if your opponent can create a counterattack that wins a piece. Sometimes it's better to consolidate.
notes.plans: Play b6 to secure the bishop and maintain the solid position.

notes.explains: White's Bc2 allowed a crushing knight maneuver to d4, attacking the queen and bishop. After Qd2, Black simply takes on c4, and there is no easy way to defend the pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated, look for ways to exploit the weaknesses with centralized knights.
notes.plans: Take the c4 pawn and continue to press, as White's position collapses.

notes.explains: Fischer's strategic play with Bg4 was impressive, and although he didn't play perfectly, he made no serious mistakes afterward, while his opponent blundered.
notes.teaches: In chess, consistency and avoiding mistakes are often more important than finding the absolute best move. A solid strategic plan can outlast your opponent's errors.

notes.explains: In the Hyperaccelerated Dragon, Black plays …g6 before committing the knight to c6, which prevents White from sidestepping into the Rossolimo with Bb5. The key difference from the Accelerated Dragon is that Black's knight is not on c6, so White gains more control over the d4 square.
notes.teaches: The move order matters: playing g6 immediately avoids certain White setups but concedes central control. Understanding these nuances helps you choose the right move order based on your preferred positions.
notes.plans: Black should be ready for White's central push d4, and aim to develop the bishop to g7 and maintain flexible pawn structure.

notes.explains: White's h5 attempt is a tricky but objectively dubious move; it gives Black a slight edge if handled correctly, though it can be a practical surprise.
notes.teaches: Not every aggressive-looking move is sound; evaluate objectively and be ready to punish overextensions.
notes.plans: If White plays h5, Black should respond by controlling the h5 square with moves like ...g6 or ...Bg7, preventing White from gaining space.

notes.explains: In the Nimzo-Indian, after d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4, White has several options. The three covered here are Nf3 (Three Knights), Bg5 (Leningrad), and g3 (Romanishin). The Romanishin often transposes to Catalan-like positions.
notes.teaches: Recognize the branching of the Nimzo-Indian and the key move orders. White's choice of g3 signals a fianchetto setup, which can lead to structures similar to the Catalan.
notes.plans: For Black, be ready to choose between solid development (castling) or the more forcing ...c5 lines.

notes.explains: In the Romanishin, after g3, Black's solid option is …O-O. White plays Bg2, and Black strikes with …d5, fighting for the center. The downside for White is that the c4-pawn becomes vulnerable, as Black can capture it with ...dxc4.
notes.teaches: When White fianchettoes the king's bishop in a Queen's pawn opening, the c4-pawn can become a target. Black should be alert to ...dxc4 to win a pawn, though White may get compensation.
notes.plans: Black can take on c4 and then develop, while White tries to regain the pawn and build pressure. The resulting positions are balanced but with dynamic chances.

notes.explains: In the line where Black plays ...c5 and ...cxd4, White avoids taking with the queen due to ...Nc6 with tempo. Instead, White develops with Nf3 and Bg2, then after ...d5, White liquidates the center with cxd5, and play becomes forcing.
notes.teaches: In these theoretical lines, precise move order is crucial. Do not be tempted by natural captures if they allow the opponent a tempo. Learn the forcing sequences to avoid mistakes.
notes.plans: Black's main continuation is ...Bxc3, leading to a known structure where both sides have chances. White must be careful about the e2-pawn and the safety of the king.

notes.explains: In this forcing line after Black takes on c3 with check, White recaptures, and Black's bishop on a6 attacks e2. Taking on e2 is a mistake because White can play c4, attacking the queen and knight, and after the tactical sequence White ends up with two bishops for a rook, which is winning.
notes.teaches: In sharp tactical variations, always check if a tempting capture allows the opponent to create a double attack or gain material advantage. Sometimes the 'obvious' capture is a trap.
notes.plans: Instead of taking on e2, Black should play Queen c5, maintaining the pressure and keeping the position balanced.

notes.explains: After the forcing sequence, the position reaches a theoretical tabiya where both sides have equal material (two rooks, queen, and light-squared bishop each). White has two isolated pawns, which gives Black a slight structural edge, but engines consider it dead equal.
notes.teaches: In equal material positions, pawn structure can be the deciding factor for human play, but engines often see dynamic compensation. Recognizing when a position is theoretically equal helps in choosing a plan.
notes.plans: Black can aim to exploit White's isolated pawns in the endgame, while White should seek active piece play to compensate.

notes.explains: Black has a choice between playing g5 immediately or castling. The move g5 is a theoretical attempt to force the bishop to g3, but it may be unnecessary. Castling and playing a normal game, with moves like e5 or Kd8, seems more natural and keeps the bishop on h4, which is not well placed.
notes.teaches: In the opening, don't rush to force a trade of a good piece if you can simply develop and maintain pressure. Sometimes the opponent's 'bad' piece is not actually bad if it can't be exploited.
notes.plans: Black can consider castling kingside and then playing e5 to expand in the center, while White might try to play f3 and Bf2 to give the bishop a better diagonal.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian line, Black's early ...g5 aims to prevent White's bishop from going to d3, which would be a strong setup. If White instead plays Be2, Black can choose between ...g5 (aggressive) or castling, with castling leading to a more comfortable game.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop wants a strong square like d3, a quick pawn move like ...g5 can stop it, but you must weigh the weakening of your kingside against the positional gain.
notes.plans: If White castles kingside, Black can later expand with ...g5, ...Nh5, and ...f5, while also preparing to pressure the d4 pawn with moves like ...Bd7, ...Qb6, and ...Rc8.

notes.explains: After the sequence with ...g5, Bg3, ...Nh5, White's bishop is misplaced, and Black can exploit the doubled pawns on the kingside. The position remains slightly better for Black despite engine evaluations.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns can be a long-term asset if they are not immediately weak; here they give Black a target and a structural advantage to exploit.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade pieces and use the doubled pawns as a hook for later pressure, while keeping the position closed to limit White's counterplay.

notes.explains: In the Three Knights variation, Black has several viable responses: ...d5 transposes to the Queen's Gambit Declined, ...c5 leads to a Romanishin-like setup, ...b6 is the most flexible Nimzo-Indian move, and castling is the simplest. Each has different characteristics.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple good moves, choose the one that best fits your style and the specific nuances of the position; transpositions can be a key tool.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...c5, White can transpose to the Romanishin with g3, while ...b6 invites a Queen's Indian setup where White must choose the nature of the game.

notes.explains: After ...b6, White has several good moves: Bg5 (Leningrad), e3, Qb3, and Qc2. The queen moves aim to recapture on c3 with the queen, but they block the dark-squared bishop and weaken the diagonal, so they are less appealing.
notes.teaches: When a move has a clear idea (like recapturing with the queen), check if it has hidden drawbacks such as blocking a piece or weakening a key diagonal.
notes.plans: White can choose between Bg5 to fight for e4, or e3 for a simple development; Black should be ready for either and maintain flexibility.

notes.explains: After e3, Black can reach a simple and flexible setup with ...d6, ...c5, and ...Nf6, keeping the bishop on g7 and preparing ...d5 or ...d6. This gives Black a comfortable game.
notes.teaches: A flexible pawn structure and a well-placed bishop can compensate for a lack of immediate activity; sometimes simple development is best.
notes.plans: Black aims to play ...d5 or ...d6, with ...Re8 and ...Bf8 to reposition the bishop if needed, while White must find a plan to create pressure.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian line, White's early e3 is somewhat passive; Black can aim for a simple setup with d3, castling, and c5, or more actively with Ne4, followed by f5, creating a Dutch-like structure with a knight on e4 and a fianchettoed bishop.
notes.teaches: When Black has a knight on e4 in the Nimzo-Indian, the move f5 is a common pattern to build a kingside attack and challenge White's center.
notes.plans: Black should consider either the solid setup with d3 and c5, or the aggressive Ne4 followed by f5, depending on preference.

notes.explains: After White plays Nf3, the most straightforward try is Bg5, pinning the knight. Black can respond with h6, and if White retreats Bh4, Black can play g5 and later f5, with the bishop already on b7, making the position slightly better defended. If Black avoids this hyper-aggressive setup, they risk being worse.
notes.teaches: Bg5 is a challenging move because it forces Black to either accept a slightly worse position or enter sharp, risky lines with g5 and f5.
notes.plans: Black should be prepared to play the aggressive g5 and f5 plan, or else face a passive position.

notes.explains: Queen's pawn openings are far more transpositional than e4 openings; for example, you rarely see a French transpose to an Italian, but in d4 openings, move orders often lead to different defenses.
notes.teaches: Be flexible in your opening repertoire and learn the key transpositions, as they allow you to steer the game into positions you know well.
notes.plans: Build general opening knowledge by studying multiple variations and their interconnections, rather than only memorizing your own lines.

notes.explains: Understanding transpositions improves your overall chess by giving you better general knowledge and helping you see what you can transpose to from your own openings.
notes.teaches: It is not necessary to know every opening deeply, but having a broad understanding of how openings connect can improve your play and adaptability.
notes.plans: Continue studying different openings and their transpositions to deepen your understanding and improve your decision-making.

notes.explains: In the Advance Caro-Kann, after e4 c6 d4 d5 e5, White gains space and piece activity, but Black's structure is solid and not easily attacked. The position is double-edged.
notes.teaches: The Advance Variation is a space-gaining setup for White, but Black's solid pawn structure provides counterbalancing safety.
notes.plans: White aims to exploit space and activity; Black seeks to undermine the center and develop harmoniously.

notes.explains: After …c5, Black sacrifices a pawn to open the position and attack White's center. White's pawn on e5 is weakened, and the move f4 is often prevented, undermining White's central control.
notes.teaches: A pawn sacrifice can be used to disrupt the opponent's center and gain activity, even if the pawn is not immediately regained.
notes.plans: Black aims for rapid development and pressure against White's center; White should consider whether to accept the pawn and how to consolidate.

notes.explains: In the main line after …Bf5, Black prepares to develop the light-squared bishop before closing the position with e6, creating a pawn triangle similar to the Slav Defense. This solves the problem of the 'bad' bishop.
notes.teaches: Developing the problem bishop before locking the pawn structure is a key idea in many openings, avoiding a passive piece.
notes.plans: Black will solidify with e6, forming a resilient structure; White will use his space to maneuver and prepare breaks.

notes.explains: The main move for White is Nf3, known as the Short Variation, popularized in the 1990s. It is a positional approach: White develops quietly, castles kingside, and aims for a slight central advantage.
notes.teaches: In the Advance Caro-Kann, a flexible, positional setup can be more effective than immediate aggression.
notes.plans: White will develop pieces, castle, and prepare central breaks; Black will aim for ...c5 to challenge the center.

notes.explains: After Nf3, Black has options like …Nd7 or the immediate …c5. The ...c5 break is a typical way to attack White's center, and after Be3 cxd4 Nxd4, Black can continue with ...Nc7, pressuring the knight.
notes.teaches: The ...c5 break is a standard method to challenge White's pawn center in the Advance Caro-Kann.
notes.plans: Black seeks to open the position and create counterplay; White must decide how to maintain the center.

notes.explains: In the line after c5, if Black plays cxd4 and White recaptures with the knight, Black can play Knight to c7 to attack the bishop. Black is happy to trade this bishop because it is a strong piece for White, and Black's knight can recapture favorably.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong bishop, it is often good to exchange it, especially if the recapture improves your piece activity or removes a key defender.
notes.plans: Black should consider exchanging the light-squared bishop for White's knight, as this simplifies the position and reduces White's attacking potential.

notes.explains: After White plays c4 in response to Black's c5, Black must be careful not to take the d4 pawn. Taking on d4 is weakening because it allows White to strike at Black's central structure. Instead, Black should either play Knight to c6 to solidify, or take on c4 and after Bishop takes c4, Black is fine because White cannot easily play d5 to improve.
notes.teaches: In such pawn structures, avoid capturing a pawn if it opens up your king or weakens your central pawn chain. Sometimes it is better to maintain tension and develop harmoniously.
notes.plans: Black should choose between Knight to c6 or cxd4 (taking on c4) depending on the position, but avoid taking on d4. If White takes on c5, Black can get activity for the pawn.

notes.explains: To study this opening, it is recommended to look at games of strong players who have played the Caro-Kann, such as Nigel Short and David Navara. Their games illustrate the typical plans and ideas discussed.
notes.teaches: Studying master games is an excellent way to learn opening theory and typical middlegame plans. It helps to see how the ideas are applied in practice.
notes.plans: Review games by top Caro-Kann players to understand the nuances of the Short Variation and the resulting middlegame structures.

notes.explains: In the main line of the Advanced Caro-Kann after Bc4-e2, White's light-squared bishop is often traded or pushed back. Black aims to develop quickly, possibly exchanging this bishop or forcing it to g7 with h6, then playing Na5 to challenge it.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann, Black should not fear exchanging the light-squared bishop; it's often a key to gaining counterplay. The bishop can be given up or driven back to a passive square.
notes.plans: Black typically plays c5, places the knight on c6, and prepares to attack the d4 pawn, which becomes a central weakness.

notes.explains: The Wonder Wheel Attack (Nc3) is an aggressive white setup aiming for a swift kingside attack. Black often sacrifices a pawn for queenside and central initiative, and despite being down material, Black can be slightly better.
notes.teaches: When facing a kingside attack, Black should seek counterplay in the center and queenside, even at the cost of a pawn, as long as the initiative compensates.
notes.plans: Black plays d6, and if White plays g4, Black responds Bg6, then Nge2 preparing Nf4. Black plays c5, accepting the loss of the h-pawn to disrupt White's central control.

notes.explains: In the line with g4, after Bg6 and Nge2, Black plays c5 and h5. If White plays Nf4, Black must not allow the bishop to be taken on g6, as that would expose the king. Instead, Bh7 gives up the h-pawn but keeps the king safe.
notes.teaches: Never allow your bishop to be trapped if it leads to a compromised king position. Sometimes giving up a pawn is necessary to maintain safety and counterplay.
notes.plans: After Nh5, Black plays Nxd4, striking in the center. Despite being a pawn down, Black has initiative on the queenside and center, while White's knight on h5 is misplaced and the e5 pawn is weak.

notes.explains: The Tal Variation (h4) in the Advanced Caro-Kann threatens to trap the bishop with g4. Black must play h5 to prevent g4. White then expands on the queenside with c4, gaining space on both sides.
notes.teaches: When facing a space-grabbing setup, Black must be precise with move orders to avoid falling into passive positions. Never allow the opponent to trap a piece without compensation.
notes.plans: Black should not take on c4; instead, play e6, Nc6, Nge7, and Nf5 to solidify. White may prepare f3-g4 to push the bishop back or play Qb3 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: In the Advance Caro-Kann, White can expand on both wings with c4 and f4, grabbing space while keeping the advanced pawns safe. Black should not take on c4, as White can solidify with b3 and develop pieces to c3 and e7.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, avoid unnecessary pawn captures that allow the opponent to consolidate; instead, maintain the pawn chain and develop pieces to support it.
notes.plans: White can prepare f3 and g4 to challenge Black's light-squared bishop, or play Qb3 to provoke Qb6 and then c4, forcing a queen trade and weakening Black's bishop on f8.

notes.explains: In the Bronstein Variation (Ne2), White's move looks passive but aims to challenge Black's bishop with Ng3 and then h4, striking on the kingside. Black must play a6 or develop, and after a6, White plays Ng3, Bg6, h4, h5, Be2, c5, Black gets counterplay.
notes.teaches: A move that seems quiet can have a deep idea; always look for ways to challenge your opponent's most active pieces.
notes.plans: Black should not take the h5 pawn because White's pieces become loose; instead, Black can play Qb6, attacking b2, d4, and the knight, leaving White unable to defend everything.

notes.explains: The move Bd3 is a common mistake: after Bxd3, Qxd3, e6, Black has gotten rid of his worst piece and solidified, while White's queen is misplaced on d3. Black is at least equal.
notes.teaches: Do not develop your queen early to a square where it can be attacked or where it blocks your own pieces; it is often better to keep the queen flexible.
